slides.title: Module 1 · Foundation · Unit 1
slides.notes:
UNIT 1 · BEHAVIOURAL STRATEGY FUNDAMENTALS
Module 1 · Foundation · Unit 1 · Unscored

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Welcome the room and name the programme.
Say: "Welcome to Strategy2Results®. Collective Intelligence for Execution. Where Strategy Meets the People Who Execute It."
Say: "Strategy2Results® is a structured leadership certification programme designed to equip senior leaders with the behavioural intelligence, cross-functional perspective and execution discipline to translate strategic intent into measurable organisational results, consistently and collectively."

2. Show the architecture of the programme.
Say: "The programme is underpinned by three integrated pillars: Direction, Influence and Grounding, which we call DIG. Each builds on the last to produce a leader who understands strategy and actively integrates it across the enterprise."
Say: "The programme runs across four modules. Module 1 · Foundation, which is this unit, Behavioural Strategy Fundamentals. Module 2 · Direction. Module 3 · Influence. Module 4 · Grounding. The Foundation module is the prerequisite for all that follows: it establishes the behavioural and cognitive literacy that every later unit requires."
Say: "Foundation establishes the behavioural basis of strategy: how human judgement, bias and emotional climate shape the decisions an executive team makes. Unit 1 is the single unit of this module. Its Problem Charter sets up the simulated company each of your groups will lead through every later unit."

3. Give the line that carries the whole programme.
Say: "The quality of your strategy is a direct function of the quality of the thinking environment in which it was made. Strategy2Results® is designed to build that environment, deliberately."

4. Explain the certification.
Say: "What you earn is CESI: Certified Enterprise Strategy Integrator. The designation recognises leaders who have demonstrated the capacity to operate beyond the boundaries of their own function: to see the enterprise whole, to integrate competing priorities into coherent direction, and to create the conditions in which strategy moves from intent to execution."
Say: "It is a practice credential, earned through application, peer challenge and demonstrated integration across the four modules of the programme."
Say: "CESI holders are equipped to navigate strategic decisions through multiple executive perspectives simultaneously; identify and interrupt cognitive bias at the point of decision; translate enterprise strategy into executable, cross-functional priority frameworks; build and sustain leadership cultures where honest challenge and collective intelligence are the norm; hold their own function accountable to enterprise outcomes; and diagnose execution failure at its source: thinking, alignment and process."

5. Say who the programme is for.
Say: "Strategy2Results® is designed for senior leaders who carry enterprise-level responsibility, whether they hold a CXO title or a role that functions at that level. It is for leaders who are already capable within their function and ready for the next level of challenge: leading at the level of the whole."
Say: "It is particularly valuable for Executive Team Members, CXO leaders who need to align across functions and translate board-level strategy into enterprise execution; Senior Leaders on the Rise, high-potential leaders preparing for executive roles who need an enterprise-wide perspective before stepping into it; and Strategy and Governance Teams, leaders responsible for planning, the strategy office or enterprise performance who need the tools to drive integration and execution quality."
Say: "Strategy2Results® is a practice you develop, and a capability your organisation keeps."

6. Bridge to the outcomes.
Say: "Let us look at what this first unit sets out to build in you."

slides.title: Key Learning Outcomes
slides.notes:
KEY LEARNING OUTCOMES

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the three outcomes aloud.
Say: "By the end of this unit you will be able to:"
Say: "One. Critically examine the influence of human judgement and organisational dynamics on strategic decision-making."
Say: "Two. Recognise the behavioural conditions that strengthen or weaken objectivity, decision quality and organisational performance."
Say: "Three. Interpret strategic issues from an integrated enterprise perspective."

2. Place the unit inside its module.
Say: "These three outcomes serve the Foundation module as a whole. The module sets out to strengthen the objectivity of strategic decisions by recognising how human judgement and organisational dynamics shape them; to cultivate a decision climate in which leaders examine evidence and assumptions before committing to strategic choices; and to lead collective decision-making that converts diverse executive perspectives into sound enterprise judgement."

3. Set the tone for the unit.
Say: "Unit 1 is unscored. Its value depends on candour. You will be asked to name your own biases before you challenge anyone else's."

4. Bridge to the unit journey.
Say: "Each section of the unit carries two learning outcomes of its own. Here is the journey."

slides.title: Competency being developed
slides.notes:
COMPETENCY BEING DEVELOPED

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:
1. Name the competency this unit develops: Behavioural Strategic Decision-Making.
2. Explain what it means in practice: The competent leader recognises how bias, emotion and functional perspective shape strategic choices. They bring diverse executive views together to reach sound enterprise judgement.
3. Read the three skills. Say: "Your reflections in this unit show how far you are developing each of these skills."
4. Keep this for your preparation: Unit 1 carries no mark. Your reading of each participant's reflections shows which of these skills they evidence.

slides.title: The Unit Journey
slides.notes:
THE UNIT JOURNEY

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Walk the six sections on the slide.
Say: "Unit 1 runs in six sections. Each one builds on the last, so the unit is cumulative."
Say: "Section 1 · Orientation, the Overview: where you start, your learning intention and the challenge you bring to the programme."
Say: "Section 2 · Awareness, the What: how human thinking, functional expertise and cognitive bias shape strategic judgement."
Say: "Section 3 · Intelligence, the Why: how functional bias diverts strategy, and what poor behavioural awareness costs the enterprise."
Say: "Section 4 · Extrapolating, the Where: where bias and emotional climate act across the strategy journey."
Say: "Section 5 · Integration, the Collective: the pillars and institutional practices that turn individual thinking into collective intelligence."
Say: "Section 6 · Application, In Practice: you assess your own bias profile, and each group sets out the challenge it will address in its Problem Charter."

2. Explain why the order matters.
Say: "Unit 1 establishes the behavioural foundation for the whole programme. We examine how judgement, bias and emotional climate shape the strategies organisations choose, and we practise recognising these forces in our own leadership teams. Every later unit relies on the shared vocabulary we build here."

3. Bridge to Section 1.
Say: "We start with Orientation."

slides.title: Section 1 · Orientation — Overview
slides.notes:
SECTION 1 · ORIENTATION — OVERVIEW

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
This is a scene-setting section. Do not rush it. The quality of engagement throughout the rest of the unit depends on participants understanding why they are here and what they are being asked to do differently. You open with the problem the programme solves (next slide), explain how participants learn through the executive role simulation, agree the ground rules for candour and confidentiality, and close with each participant's learning intention.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Recognise how human judgement shapes the way your team debates, decides and sets organisational direction.
2. Articulate a personal learning intention anchored in a current leadership or strategic challenge.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Introduce behavioural strategy in plain terms.
Say: "Behavioural strategy sits at the intersection of cognitive psychology and strategic management. By incorporating psychology into strategy, it recognises that strategy is deeply human."
Say: "This field bridges cognitive and social insights to improve decision quality. It challenges the assumption that leaders think rationally when charting organisational direction and, more importantly, equips them to do something about it."
Say: "As you progress through the Strategy2Results® process, you will begin to recognise patterns in how your team debates, how your organisation makes decisions, and how your own mental models shape the strategy your organisation ultimately pursues."

2. Explain how you will learn: the Executive Leadership Perspective Simulation.
Say: "The most powerful feature of the Strategy2Results® programme is how you learn."
Say: "Each of you takes an executive role outside your own function, and together your group forms a Simulated Enterprise Executive Team, the SEET: CEO, CFO, COO, CHRO, CTO, CMO, CCO, CPO, CRO or CSO. You analyse each unit's challenge through that executive's priorities, concerns and strategic perspective."
Say: "I will hold you to that role discipline from this first unit. It is the mechanism through which the programme builds collective intelligence. By inhabiting another executive's perspective with rigour, as a genuine analytical discipline, you develop the capacity to anticipate cross-functional implications, surface hidden dependencies, and make decisions that hold at the enterprise level as well as within your own function."
Say: "This is what separates strategic leaders from functional experts: the ability to think from a seat you do not occupy, and to do it well enough that the person who does occupy it trusts your reasoning."

3. Agree the ground rules for candour and confidentiality.
Say: "Before we go further, we agree how we will work together. What is said in this room about your organisations and your colleagues stays in this room. And we commit to candour: we name our own biases before we name anyone else's."
Ask: "What else do we need to agree so that everyone can speak honestly here?"
Listen for: confidentiality, respect for different seats, permission to challenge, no point-scoring. These ground rules carry through all twelve units.

4. Bridge to the opening research.
Say: "Let us begin with the problem this programme solves."

slides.title: Research Statistics
slides.notes:
OPENING THE SESSION · THE PROBLEM THIS PROGRAMME SOLVES

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the research on the slide.
Say: "Research consistently shows that 60–90% of strategies fail in delivery. The causes may appear different across organisations, but they tend to sit within three areas of strategy failure: Direction, Influence and Grounding."
Say: "Let us walk through each of the three."

2. Direction Failure.
Say: "Direction failure: the organisation is not thinking about strategy with sufficient clarity, coherence and enterprise perspective."
Deepen, say: "Organisations often let functions, departments and individuals pursue objectives without enough understanding of how those objectives contribute to the larger organisational intent. The result can be excellent local performance without coherent enterprise progress. Start with the whole, then locate each part within it."
(Insight: The whole before the parts. Source: Journal, 3 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Say: "Here is what happens when the organisation is not thinking about strategy with sufficient clarity, coherence and enterprise perspective."
Say: "First, leaders think in functional silos. What it costs: fragmented priorities, competing KPIs and decisions that optimise functions at the expense of the enterprise. What S2R® builds: enterprise perspective, the capacity to think beyond one's function and understand strategy from every seat at the table."
Say: "Second, cognitive bias distorts decisions invisibly. What it costs: poor capital allocation, strategic inertia, suppressed innovation and purpose drift. What S2R® builds: behavioural intelligence, the ability to recognise and challenge bias before it becomes a strategic cost."

3. Influence Failure.
Say: "Influence failure: people, decisions and organisational conditions are not aligned behind the strategy."
Deepen, say: "Strategies, values, policies and governance structures may all exist formally while everyday decisions follow an entirely different logic. Test whether those artefacts meaningfully govern resource allocation, priorities and behaviour."
(Insight: Symbolic compliance. Source: Journal, 1 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Say: "When people, decisions and organisational conditions are not aligned behind the strategy, two things manifest."
Say: "First, emotional climate is left unmanaged. What it costs: fear and ego replace curiosity; honest challenge disappears; groupthink fills the gap. What S2R® builds: climate leadership, the ability to create conditions in which people can challenge, contribute and make better strategic decisions."
Say: "Second, accountability stays structural and does not become cultural. What it costs: leaders protect their functions, progress is reported without being owned, and strategy reviews become performance theatre. What S2R® builds: strategic ownership, leaders who carry responsibility for the whole while remaining accountable for their part."

4. Grounding Failure.
Say: "Grounding failure: strategic intent does not translate into coordinated execution and sustained results."
Deepen, say: "Organisations frequently possess capable functions, talented individuals and substantial resources and still struggle to convert them into collective results. The problem may lie in the quality of the connections between the parts. Strategy must determine how those contributions fit together around the outcome the organisation is trying to create."
(Insight: The connections between the parts. Source: Journal, 4 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Say: "This is what you are likely to get: strategy is cascaded without being integrated. What it costs: strategic intent fragments as it moves through functions, levels and teams; dependencies are missed and execution energy dissipates. What S2R® builds: integration discipline, the ability to connect strategic intent, organisational contributions, decisions and action across the enterprise."

5. Close the opening.
Say: "These are predictable failure points in the journey from strategy to results. S2R® develops leaders who can recognise them, intervene in them and integrate across them, so that strategy produces results."

6. Ask for the learning intention.
Say: "Hold one question as we move on: what brings you here? What is one thing about your leadership or your organisation's strategy that you most want to understand differently by the end of this unit?"
Ask two or three participants to share.

7. Bridge to the section close.
Say: "Strategic judgement begins with the person exercising it. Your learning intention anchors this unit in a challenge you lead today. Next, Section 2 examines what behavioural strategy is."

slides.notes:

slides.title: Section 2 · Awareness — What
slides.notes:
SECTION 2 · AWARENESS — WHAT
What Behavioural Strategy Is · 2.1 · 2.2 · 2.3 · 2.4

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
This section establishes the conceptual foundation. Participants are introduced to what behavioural strategy is (2.1), how individual thinking is structured (2.2), how collective thinking breaks down through functional bias (2.3), and what the 20 most common cognitive biases look like in practice (2.4). Expect some resistance: experienced leaders often feel they already know this. The role of the facilitator is to make the content feel personally relevant.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Recognise how intuitive thinking, functional expertise and cognitive bias shape strategic judgement.
2. Identify the patterns of bias most active in your leadership team, your team members and your organisation.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Name what the section covers.
Say: "Section 2 examines what behavioural strategy is: how intuitive thinking, functional expertise and cognitive bias shape strategic judgement."

2. Bridge to the opening question.
Say: "Before we define anything, I want to start with the person in the mirror."

slides.title: Starting with the person in the mirror
slides.notes:
STARTING WITH THE PERSON IN THE MIRROR

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Ask the question on the slide.
Ask: "When you make a strategic decision, how much of it do you believe is purely rational?"

2. Define what rational means here.
Say: "In this case, rational means making a decision based only on facts, evidence and logic, without being influenced by emotions, assumptions, past experiences or personal preferences."

3. Take responses and hold the tension.
Take two or three responses. Do not resolve the question. Hold the tension: this prepares the ground for the definition that follows.

4. Bridge to 2.1.
Say: "Keep your answer in mind. The definition of behavioural strategy will test it."

slides.title: 2.1a · Defining Behavioural Strategy
slides.notes:
2.1a · DEFINING BEHAVIOURAL STRATEGY

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Land the key concept.
Say: "Strategic decisions are shaped by the information available to us and by how we think, interpret and respond to that information. This is the central pivot of the unit; everything else builds from it."

2. Explain what behavioural strategy is.
Say: "Behavioural strategy applies insights from cognitive and social psychology to strategic management. At its core, it recognises that strategy is a human process. People make strategic choices, and people interpret, respond to and ultimately execute those choices."
Say: "This means people sit on both sides of strategy: the people who shape it and the people who must make it happen."
Say: "Leaders do not make strategic decisions through logic and analysis alone. Their thinking is influenced by cognitive biases, assumptions, emotions, past experiences and social dynamics, often without conscious awareness. Equally, once a strategy has been decided, its success depends on how others understand it, respond to it, make decisions around it and behave in delivering it. Behavioural strategy therefore brings the human dimension into both strategy formulation and execution."
Add: "The discipline is grounded in the work of scholars such as Daniel Kahneman and advanced in the field of behavioural strategy by thinkers like Olivier Sibony. It acknowledges that strategic choices are the final output of invisible mental filters (shortcuts, ignored data and trusted patterns) that operate beneath the level of conscious analysis."

3. Read the core question on the slide.
Point to the two cards.
Say: "Traditional strategy asks: what should we do?"
Read aloud: "Behavioural strategy asks first: how does the way we think shape what we believe we should do — and what will shape how people respond and act?"
Ask the group to sit with the question for a moment before you go on.
Say: "The focus expands from the strategic decision itself to the human thinking and behaviour surrounding it."

4. Give the formal definition.
Say: "Powell, Lovallo and Fox (2011) define behavioural strategy as the application of cognitive and social psychology to strategic management theory and practice."
Point to the definition at the foot of the slide.
Read aloud: "The S2R® definition: Behavioural Strategy is the application of behavioural science to understand and improve how people think, decide and behave throughout the process of strategy, from shaping strategic choices to delivering results."
Ask: "Does this definition change how you understood strategy before walking in today?"

5. Connect the definition to execution.
Deepen, say: "Strategy execution requires more than communicating priorities. People need to understand where the organisation is going, what the larger outcome is, and how their particular contribution connects to it. Without that connection, organisations can generate significant activity while producing fragmented results."
(Insight: Contribution and the larger outcome. Source: Journal, 3 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

6. Bridge to 2.1b.
Say: "Three phrases in that definition carry the whole idea: how we think, how we decide, how we behave."

slides.title: 2.1b · Three Phrases That Carry The Idea
slides.notes:
2.1b · THREE PHRASES THAT CARRY THE IDEA

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open the three phrases.
Say: "We have defined behavioural strategy. Now I want us to slow down and look at three parts of that definition more closely. They give us a simple way of understanding where the human dimension enters strategy: how we think, how we decide, how we behave."

2. How we think.
Say: "How we think is how we make sense of what we see or do: the assumptions, mental models and biases that shape what we notice, how we interpret it and what we believe it means."
Say: "We do not simply absorb information exactly as it is presented to us. We interpret it. What we notice, what we pay attention to, what we dismiss and the meaning we give to information are influenced by the thinking we bring with us. This is why two people can look at the same evidence and reach very different conclusions."
Deepen, say: "When two groups read the same evidence and reach opposite conclusions, the difference usually sits in the interpretive framework each brings to it. Every strategic assessment is shaped partly by the evidence and partly by the assumptions of the people assessing it. Honest strategy separates the two."
(Insight: Same evidence, different conclusions. Source: Journal, 7 March 2026 — Professional Insights)
Say: "So the first behavioural question in strategy is: how are we thinking about what we are seeing or doing?"

3. How we decide.
Say: "How we decide is how we turn understanding into choice and commitment: the judgements, trade-offs and influences that shape what we choose, what we prioritise and what we commit to doing."
Say: "What we believe about a situation eventually has to become a choice. We decide what matters, what takes priority, what we will pursue, what we will leave behind and, importantly, what we are prepared to commit ourselves to doing. Those choices are shaped by the information available to us and also by our judgement, perceptions, relationships, emotions and the influence of others."
Deepen, say: "Decisions made under emotional pressure can create consequences far beyond the immediate issue. Emotion, group reinforcement and reputational anxiety can drive consequential decisions without sufficient reflection. Separate the presenting problem from the emotional reaction around it and test whether the proposed response is proportionate."
(Insight: Emotion in the decision. Source: Journal, 13 August 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Say: "So the second question becomes: what is shaping the choices and commitments we are making?"

4. How we behave.
Say: "How we behave is how our commitments become action: how people respond, contribute, coordinate and act, which determines whether we deliver and achieve the intended outcomes."
Say: "A decision produces a result only once people act on it. People still have to respond to it, translate it into their own contribution, coordinate with others and act consistently with what has been agreed. This is where our commitments become visible."
Deepen, say: "The gap between stated intention and actual behaviour is one of the most revealing leadership diagnostics available. Build accountability into the space between the commitment and the moment of execution, so that what people sincerely intend is what they do when the pressure of circumstances arrives."
(Insight: The gap between intention and action. Source: Journal, 20 February 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Say: "So the third question is: are our behaviours actually carrying our commitments through to the intended outcomes?"

5. Land the three phrases.
Point to the three cards.
Say: "How we think shapes how we decide. How we decide shapes what we commit to. How we behave determines whether those commitments become results."
Read the banner aloud: "If we do not understand what shapes how we think, decide and behave, we cannot know whether we are moving towards or away from our intended outcomes."

6. Ask the room.
Ask: "Which of these three, how we think, how we decide or how we behave, presents the greatest challenge in your organisation today?"
Allow a short pair discussion before moving on.

7. Bridge to 2.2.
Say: "We begin with the first of these: how we think. The task is to understand what is shaping how we think, as well as what we think."

slides.title: 2.2 · Two Systems Of Thinking
slides.notes:
2.2 · TWO SYSTEMS OF THINKING

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open with the question.
Say: "We have just said that how we think shapes how we decide. So the next question is: how do we actually think?"
Say: "One useful way of understanding this comes from Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman's work on dual-process thinking. At times we think quickly and intuitively. At other times we slow down and think deliberately and analytically. He describes these as System 1 and System 2 thinking."
Say: "We need both. The strategic discipline is recognising which one is shaping our judgement, and whether the situation requires us to slow down and examine that judgement more carefully. For anyone with a mandate for strategy, recognising which system is dominant is the difference between a reactive impulse and a disciplined, well thought through choice."

2. System 1: fast thinking.
Point to the System 1 card.
Say: "System 1 is automatic, intuitive and pattern-based. It is the thinking that happens quickly, often without us consciously working through every step. It operates below conscious awareness, draws heavily on experience, patterns, associations and emotion, and produces rapid, confident judgements. It is dominant in high-pressure strategy sessions, and it is vulnerable to cognitive biases."
Say: "This is why an experienced leader can walk into a situation and immediately feel that something is wrong, or see an opportunity before others do. That intuition can be extremely valuable. Because System 1 works quickly, it can also rely on assumptions and mental shortcuts that we have not examined."
Example, say: "A leader hears about a new market opportunity and almost immediately thinks: 'This is something we should pursue.' That judgement may contain years of valuable experience. It may also contain assumptions that have not yet been tested. So the better question is: when should we trust our gut, and when should we test it?"

3. System 2: slow thinking.
Point to the System 2 card.
Say: "System 2 is deliberate, analytical and effortful. It is what happens when we deliberately slow our thinking down. We examine evidence, question assumptions, compare alternatives, weigh options and trade-offs, and work through complexity. It is slower and more reliable for complex problems. It requires attention and effort, which is why we do not operate this way all the time. It is easily overridden by System 1 under time pressure, and it requires psychological safety to activate."
Example, say: "The leader's initial instinct may be: 'This market looks attractive.' System 2 asks: what evidence supports that? What might we be missing? What assumptions are we making? What are the alternatives? What would have to be true for this choice to succeed? System 2 tests the intuition."
Deepen, say: "Strategy is weakened when leaders become so committed to movement that they ignore capability gaps. A disciplined pause can prevent an expensive failure later."
(Insight: A disciplined pause. Source: Journal, 1 August 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

4. Land the two systems.
Say: "System 1 gives us speed. System 2 gives us scrutiny. Both have a place in strategy. The challenge arises when fast thinking produces a judgement in a situation that requires deeper examination, and we never recognise that we needed to slow down."
Read the banner aloud: "Know when System 2 is needed, and create the conditions for it to activate."

5. Ask where System 1 takes over.
Ask: "Under what conditions does System 1 tend to take over in your organisation?"
Then ask: "What does that actually look like in the meeting room?"
Listen for: time pressure, hierarchy, strong personalities, familiarity, crisis, fatigue, previous success, consensus or pressure to demonstrate action.

6. Make the key facilitation point.
Say: "Experienced leaders need intuition; pattern recognition is part of expertise. The discipline is knowing when intuition is enough and when the stakes, uncertainty or complexity require us to engage System 2 deliberately. Sometimes that requires creating the conditions to slow the room down."
Deepen, say: "Strong organisations need room to say 'We do not yet know' without reading uncertainty as incompetence. That humility improves learning and stops assumptions from hardening prematurely into facts."
(Insight: Room to say "We do not yet know". Source: Journal, 3 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

7. Show how pressure feeds System 1.
Say: "Under pressure, leaders can feel compelled to demonstrate action. Speed of response and quality of response are different things. The discipline to slow down, think clearly and act from assessed calm is one of the rarest leadership capacities."
Say: "A leader's position gives weight to what they say. A quick reaction from the most senior person in the room can become organisational direction before it was ever intended to be. Sometimes System 2 begins with something as simple as: 'Let me think about that before we decide.' That pause is a deliberate thinking discipline."

8. Leave the room with one question.
Say: "Think of a significant strategic decision you were recently involved in. Which system appeared to dominate? What conditions made that more likely?"
Then ask: "Looking back, was that the kind of thinking the decision required?"
Say: "The question to carry into every important decision is: what kind of thinking does this decision require from us?"

9. Bridge to 2.3.
Say: "If System 1 works quickly and often outside our conscious awareness, what happens when the shortcuts it relies on distort our judgement? That is where functional bias begins."

slides.title: 2.3 · Functional Bias - The Elephant Perspective
slides.notes:
2.3 · FUNCTIONAL BIAS IN STRATEGY: THE ELEPHANT PERSPECTIVE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open with a provocation.
Ask: "In your leadership team, who sees the most complete picture of the organisation's strategic reality? What does that person's role tell you?"
Allow a brief discussion.

2. Move from the individual to the table.
Say: "We have just looked at how our individual thinking shapes our judgement. Strategy is rarely shaped or delivered by one person. It is shaped around a table, by leaders responsible for different parts of the organisation, and brought to life by people across the organisation who must interpret it, respond to it and act on it."
Say: "That introduces another challenge. We may be working towards the same strategic outcome without thinking about what it requires, or how to achieve it, in the same way. One person sees a people issue. Another sees a financial issue. Another an operational issue. Another a customer issue. Same strategy. Same intended outcome. Different ways of thinking about what needs to be done."
Say: "Every executive leader develops deep expertise within their domain. That expertise drives competence, speed and confidence. It also creates invisible filters that shape what leaders notice, how they interpret information, what they prioritise and what they believe needs to be done. Left unexamined, these differences surface as execution friction: delayed decisions, misaligned KPIs, teams moving with energy in different directions."

3. Define functional bias.
Say: "Every person engages strategy from somewhere. Our roles, expertise and responsibilities give us a particular perspective. That perspective is valuable. It can also influence what we notice, what we prioritise, how we interpret a situation and what we believe should be done about it."
Read aloud: "Functional bias: the tendency to interpret a strategic issue, and what should be done about it, primarily from the perspective of our own function, expertise or area of responsibility."
Say: "Our perspective may well be right. The difficulty is that it may only be part of the picture."

4. Read the parable.
Read the parable aloud yourself, or invite a participant to read it to the group. Point to the six cards as you go.
Read aloud: "There is an old story, told in many forms across many cultures, about six men who are blind from birth. One day they are led to an elephant, an animal they have heard spoken of but never encountered, and each is invited to discover it."
Read aloud: "The first man reaches out and touches the side of the elephant. It is vast, flat and solid. 'An elephant,' he declares, 'is like a wall.' The second finds a tusk and wraps his hands around its smooth, curved length. 'Not at all,' he says. 'It is like a spear.' The third takes hold of the trunk as it curls and twists. 'You are both wrong. It is like a snake.' The fourth encircles a leg and feels the rough, pillar-like mass beneath his palms. 'It is a tree trunk.' The fifth grasps the ear and feels its wide, flat sweep. 'It is a fan.' The sixth grabs the tail. 'It is a rope.'"
Pause. Give the room a moment of quiet. Resist the urge to explain it straight away.

5. Draw out the meaning.
Say: "Each person has encountered something real. Each has evidence for what they believe. Each conclusion makes sense from where that person is standing. None has the complete picture. None is lying and none is careless. The problem begins when the part they see becomes the whole of what they believe."
Deepen, say: "Organisations can hold deep technical expertise and still make poor choices when judgement lacks the discipline of purpose. Fragmentation around personalities distorts collective direction."
(Insight: Knowledge, capability and wisdom. Source: Journal, 31 August 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

6. Bring it back to strategy.
Say: "This is what can happen in strategy. Finance may see one implication. Operations another. People and Culture another. Technology another. The frontline may experience something else entirely. Each perspective may contain something important. If each person acts only from their own interpretation, the organisation can have capable people making reasonable decisions that collectively do not add up to a coherent response."
Say: "That is where functional bias becomes a strategic problem. It shows up as competing priorities, conflicting decisions, misaligned measures, missed dependencies and teams working hard in different directions."
Deepen, say: "Finance optimises finance, HR optimises HR, operations optimises operations, and each may perform well individually while the enterprise struggles collectively. Coherence grows when people routinely ask two questions: 'What is my function responsible for?' and 'What does the organisation need from my function for the whole to succeed?'"
(Insight: Function and enterprise. Source: Journal, 3 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

7. Debrief.
Ask: "If your organisation were this elephant, what part might different functions or teams be touching?"
Allow the discussion to develop.
Then ask: "Where might people be making perfectly reasonable decisions from where they sit, but those decisions are not producing the best outcome for the whole?"
And finally: "What would have to happen for everyone around the elephant to understand more of the whole?"
Listen for: the functions that are consistently named. This often surfaces the real silo structure of the organisation.

8. Land the insight.
Say: "The classic Elephant parable illustrates a structural requirement for strategic leadership: the shift from individual accuracy to collective coherence. At the enterprise level, strategic quality is determined by an organisation's ability to surface these partial truths, hold them in tension and integrate them into a unified understanding of reality."
Ask: "What would it take in your organisation to surface, hold and integrate all those partial truths?"
Read the line at the foot of the slide: "The strategic discipline is being able to bring the depth of our own perspective without assuming that our perspective is complete."
Say: "Functional bias does not mean we abandon our expertise. We need the different perspectives."
Deepen, say: "A team that is too uniform will be blind to the moments it was never built for. When building a team, deliberately include the person who does not fit the template; that person often solves the problem no one else can see."
(Insight: The person who does not fit the template. Source: Journal, 18 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)

9. Bridge to 2.4.
Say: "The challenge is whether different perspectives can be brought together to understand the whole. There is another layer beneath where we sit: the predictable ways human judgement can become distorted. These are cognitive biases."

slides.title: 2.4 · Bias Families
slides.notes:
2.4 · THE COGNITIVE BIAS FAMILY: 20 BIASES ACROSS 4 FAMILIES

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open with the two filters.
Say: "Every strategic message passes through two human filters: the mind, which is cognition, and the heart, which is emotion. The biases in this part help us understand the mind: how human judgement can distort what we notice, interpret, assume and decide."
Say: "We have just seen that people can engage the same strategic task and think about it differently. Our roles and experience explain some of that difference. Sometimes the difference comes from the predictable ways in which human judgement can become distorted."

2. Define a cognitive bias.
Say: "A cognitive bias is a pattern in our thinking that can systematically influence how we interpret information, make judgements and arrive at decisions. It goes deeper than a single mistake. And we all have them. We are often much better at recognising bias in someone else's thinking than in our own."

3. Explain why bias matters in strategy.
Say: "Remember System 1. Our minds are constantly helping us make sense of complexity quickly. We use experience, patterns and mental shortcuts so that we do not have to analyse everything from the beginning every time. Most of the time, that is useful. Those same shortcuts can also pull our judgement in a particular direction without us realising it. That matters in strategy because the distortion can influence what we believe, what we decide and what we commit to doing."
Say: "So the question is: which biases might be influencing our thinking here?"

4. Introduce the four families.
Say: "There are many documented cognitive biases. In this programme we work with 20 biases grouped into four families, so that we can recognise them more easily in strategic situations. Each family represents a different way our judgement can be pulled away from a more considered assessment. For now, explore them. There is no need to memorise them."

5. Family 1: Action-Oriented Biases.
Say: "Action-oriented biases are the pull towards acting, committing or moving ahead. They influence how confident we feel about what we know, how positively we see the future, how much control we believe we have and how quickly we commit to action. They are Overconfidence, Optimism, Illusion of Control, Planning Fallacy and Confirmation."
Say: "The question to hold: what might be causing us to move with greater confidence or certainty than the situation warrants?"
Say: "Case in point: Steinhoff. For years, Steinhoff was celebrated for rapid growth and international expansion. Acquisition followed acquisition, and the organisation grew into a multinational retail group. In 2017, accounting irregularities came to light, triggering a dramatic collapse in market value and exposing significant governance failures."
Ask: "If we looked at this as a case in point, which bias or biases might have been at play?"
Let participants diagnose the case before you offer your reflection.
Listen for: overconfidence, optimism, illusion of control and confirmation bias.
Say: "Repeated success can strengthen confidence in the organisation's judgement and its ability to manage increasing complexity. As confidence grows, assumptions may receive less challenge and warning signals may carry less weight."
Connect it to the family. Say: "Overconfidence: has repeated success increased our confidence in our own judgement beyond what the evidence supports? Optimism: are we placing greater weight on how well this could go than on what could go wrong? Illusion of Control: are we assuming we can manage complexities and outcomes that may sit beyond our control? Planning Fallacy: are we underestimating the time, resources and complexity required to deliver what we have committed to? Confirmation: once we have committed to a direction, are we paying more attention to evidence that supports it than evidence that challenges it?"
Deepen, say: "The leader who promises the board a delivery date in the heat of the meeting, or announces a pricing change before the commercial modelling is done, shows the planning fallacy at work. One discipline: no public commitment to a number, date or outcome above an agreed threshold without a 24-hour pause."
(Insight: Committing before counting the cost. Source: Journal, 22 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Say: "Notice how these biases reinforce one another. Success can increase confidence. Confidence can strengthen optimism. Optimism can make ambitious plans appear more achievable. Once we have committed, confirmation bias can make contradictory evidence easier to explain away. The behavioural lesson: success can become part of the conditions that make overconfidence possible."
Deepen, say: "Overconfidence after a significant victory is one of the most dangerous leadership conditions. Build a habit of consultation that holds regardless of how strong the last result felt."
(Insight: Overconfidence after a win. Source: Journal, 6 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)

6. Family 2: Stability Biases.
Say: "Stability biases are the pull towards protecting, preserving or staying with what we already know. They influence how strongly we hold onto existing assumptions, investments, arrangements and positions, even as circumstances change. They are Anchoring, Status Quo, Loss Aversion, Sunk-Cost and Endowment."
Say: "The question to hold: what might we be holding onto simply because it is familiar, established or already ours?"
Say: "Case in point: Kodak. For much of the 20th century, Kodak dominated the photography industry. Its film-based business was highly profitable, and the company had built enormous capability, infrastructure and brand strength around it. In 1975, a Kodak engineer developed one of the world's first digital cameras, so Kodak had early visibility of the technology that would eventually transform photography. Digital photography presented a difficult strategic tension: moving aggressively towards digital meant embracing a technology that threatened the highly profitable film business on which Kodak's success was built. As consumers moved towards digital photography, Kodak struggled to adapt its business model quickly enough. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 2012."
Ask: "If this were a case in point, which biases might have been at play?"
Let participants diagnose the case before offering your reflection.
Listen for: status quo bias, loss aversion, anchoring and the endowment effect.
Say: "Kodak saw digital technology coming. It had participated in its development. The deeper strategic challenge was what embracing digital required Kodak to reconsider: a successful existing business, established capabilities, investments and an economic model that had served the organisation extremely well. This is where stability biases become powerful. What already exists can become the reference point from which the future is judged. What has created value can become difficult to disrupt. And what we already own can appear more valuable because it is ours."
Connect it to the family. Say: "Anchoring: are we judging the future using assumptions formed when our existing business model was still dominant? Status Quo: does staying with what we know feel safer than fundamentally changing how we create value? Loss Aversion: are we more concerned about losing the value of our existing business than capturing the value of the emerging opportunity? Sunk Cost: are previous investments influencing our willingness to redirect resources, even when circumstances have changed? Endowment Effect: are we placing greater value on our existing capabilities, assets and business model because they belong to us?"
Say: "Notice how these reinforce one another. Past success anchors our expectations around the existing business. That anchor makes the status quo feel familiar, proven and therefore safer. The prospect of disrupting what already works activates loss aversion. The more we have invested, the stronger the pull of sunk cost. And because the capabilities, assets and business are already ours, the endowment effect makes them appear more valuable and more difficult to relinquish. The more we have built around the past, the harder it can become to move towards the future."
Deepen, say: "Past evidence matters, yet it cannot substitute for present discernment. Organisations need institutional memory without becoming prisoners of historical formulas. What worked before is one input to present thinking."
(Insight: Previous success and present discernment. Source: Journal, 28 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Say: "Sometimes the greatest difficulty in responding to the future is letting go of what made us successful in the past."
Ask: "What are we protecting today because it has worked for us before?"

7. Family 3: Interest Biases.
Say: "Interest biases are the pull of our own position, interests and perspective. Our responsibilities, incentives, expertise and personal exposure can influence what we believe is best for the organisation. This can happen without deliberate self-interest. A leader can genuinely believe they are making the right strategic recommendation while their judgement is being shaped by what they are responsible for, rewarded for, know best or feel exposed by. They are Self-Interest, Silo, Incentive, Career-Risk and Perspective."
Say: "The question to hold: how might where I sit, what I know, what I am responsible for or what I stand to gain or lose be shaping my judgement? This connects directly back to the Elephant: the part of the elephant we touch can influence what we believe the whole organisation needs."
Say: "Case in point: Safaricom and the move into M-PESA. When Safaricom was developing M-PESA in Kenya, the idea represented something quite different from the traditional telecommunications business. A telecommunications company normally thinks about customers through calls, airtime, network usage and subscriber growth. M-PESA required the organisation to think beyond the interests and assumptions of a conventional mobile operator and enter financial services: building an agent network, managing cash, addressing regulation and creating a service for people who often did not have conventional bank accounts."
Say: "Imagine the strategic conversation inside such an organisation. The technology team could see a technology platform. The commercial team could see subscribers and revenue. The finance team could see investment and risk. The regulatory team could see an unfamiliar regulatory environment. The traditional telecommunications business could ask why resources should move towards something outside its established core. Yet the opportunity required these interests to be integrated around a larger enterprise opportunity."
Ask: "If this were a case in point, which interest bias could easily have prevented the organisation from seeing the opportunity?"
Say: "Remember our elephant. Each function could have looked at M-PESA and reached a perfectly reasonable conclusion from where it sat. The danger would have arisen if any one of those functional perspectives had been allowed to define the opportunity for the whole organisation. This is how interest bias can operate without anyone behaving improperly. Our responsibility influences what we pay attention to. What we are measured on influences what we protect. Our expertise influences what we consider possible."
Connect it to the family. Say: "Self-Interest: does this opportunity strengthen or threaten something I or we personally control, influence or benefit from? Silo: am I judging the opportunity primarily through what it means for my function, and missing what it could mean for the enterprise? Incentive: are the measures and targets I am accountable for influencing whether I see this opportunity as attractive? Career-Risk: would supporting an unfamiliar opportunity expose me personally if it failed? Perspective: is what I know well limiting my ability to see possibilities outside my expertise and experience?"
Say: "Notice how these reinforce one another. Our perspective shapes what we notice. Our functional position can turn that perspective into silo thinking. Our incentives reinforce which outcomes appear most important. Those interests become more personal when a decision affects our influence, resources or standing, strengthening self-interest. And when supporting a different direction could expose us personally, career-risk bias makes the familiar position easier to defend. Where we sit can gradually shape what we come to believe is best for the whole organisation, and nobody needs to be acting dishonestly. The reinforcement can happen through completely legitimate responsibilities."
Say: "Functional expertise gives us depth. Enterprise thinking helps us see beyond the interests of the function."
Ask: "What opportunity might your organisation be interpreting too narrowly because each function is looking at it from where it sits?"

8. Family 4: Social Biases.
Say: "Social biases are the pull of other people on our judgement. We do not think and decide in isolation. Who is in the room, who holds authority, what the group believes, whose voice carries weight and what feels socially acceptable can all influence what people are willing to think, say and support. They are Conformity, Authority, Groupthink, Availability and Halo Effect."
Say: "The question to hold: how might the people around us be influencing what we are willing to see, say or decide?"
Say: "Case in point: KPMG South Africa. KPMG South Africa had a long-standing relationship with companies linked to the Gupta family, providing auditing and other professional services. As concerns around the Gupta businesses and state capture intensified, KPMG came under scrutiny over work it had performed, including its audits of Gupta-linked companies and its controversial SARS report. In 2017, KPMG International conducted an investigation into the South African practice. The consequences were significant: senior leadership resigned, clients terminated relationships with the firm, and KPMG withdrew findings and recommendations from its SARS report. For a global professional-services firm whose business depends on independent judgement and professional challenge, the case raises an important behavioural question."
Ask: "If this were a case in point, which biases might have been at play?"
Listen for: authority bias, conformity, groupthink and potentially the halo effect.
Connect it to the family. Say: "Conformity: everyone around me appears comfortable with this; am I really the one who has it wrong? Authority: senior and respected people have approved this; how strongly should I challenge it? Groupthink: the group appears to agree; do I really want to be the person who reopens the issue? Availability: are the views we hear most frequently or most confidently receiving more weight than the evidence warrants? Halo Effect: does the reputation, status or previous success of this person, client or institution influence how critically we examine them?"
Say: "Social bias can operate without anyone explicitly telling us what to think. We read the room. We recognise authority. We notice which relationships matter, whose views receive support, what others are willing to challenge and what happens to people who disagree. Those signals gradually shape what people are prepared to see, say and support."
Deepen, say: "Informal social pressure can overpower formally held beliefs. No policy is needed; the presence of particular people is enough to change behaviour. This is culture operating through signals, belonging and perceived approval."
(Insight: Informal pressure. Source: Journal, 27 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Say: "Notice how these reinforce one another. The reputation or standing of a person creates a halo effect, giving their judgement greater credibility. Their seniority strengthens authority bias, making others less willing to challenge them. As fewer people challenge, conformity becomes easier. Repeated agreement develops into groupthink, where maintaining alignment becomes more important than examining alternatives. And as the same views are repeatedly heard, availability bias makes them feel increasingly representative of reality. What begins as influence can become agreement, and agreement can begin to look like evidence."
Deepen, say: "A leader who fills the room with people who agree has engineered a blind spot and called it harmony. Unwelcome accuracy is worth more than pleasant confirmation. Seek out the person willing to say what the agreeable majority will not, and protect them from the cost honesty usually carries."
(Insight: Engineered blind spots. Source: Journal, 16 June 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Ask: "Think about your own leadership table. What would someone have to risk to disagree with the most powerful person in the room?"

9. Explain bias chains.
Say: "Biases can form chains. One bias changes how we interpret the situation, which creates the conditions for another, and another. By the time the organisation reaches a decision, several biases may be reinforcing the same conclusion. This is why recognising bias early matters. The earlier we interrupt the chain, the greater our opportunity to improve the quality of judgement before it becomes commitment and action."

10. Land the four families.
Point to the four cards.
Say: "Our judgement can be pulled in different directions. Action pulls us towards moving. Stability pulls us towards staying. Interest pulls us towards our own position or perspective. Social influence pulls us towards others. And these influences can operate without us consciously recognising them. The strategic discipline is learning to recognise what may be pulling our judgement before that judgement becomes a decision, commitment or action."

11. Group reflection.
Ask: "Which of these four families do you recognise most strongly in your own thinking?"
Then ask: "Which one do you see most clearly in your organisation?"
And finally: "Can you identify a strategic decision where one of these biases may have influenced what was ultimately decided or done?"
Caution: participants may drift towards naming other people's biases. Redirect gently: "We are here to understand the patterns so we can design better processes. Where did that bias show up in your own last decision?"

12. Close the section.
Say: "While it is happening, bias often feels like experience, confidence, caution, expertise or agreement. The strategic discipline is learning to recognise what may be pulling our judgement before that judgement becomes a decision, commitment or action."

13. Bridge to Section 3.
Say: "Section 3 examines why behavioural strategy is critical, through a case of functional bias and the hidden cost of poor behavioural awareness."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
The portal describes each of the 20 biases from two angles: what it does in strategy, and the organisational signals that the bias is at play. Participants click a family card and then each bias to read the full detail.
