slides.title: Section 3 · Intelligence — Why
slides.notes:
SECTION 3 · INTELLIGENCE — WHY
Why Behavioural Strategy Is Critical · 3.1 · 3.2

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
Section 2 established what behavioural strategy is. This section answers why it matters, through a live case (3.1, MyHealth) and quantified organisational costs (3.2). Participants who were intellectually engaged in Section 2 should become personally invested here. The MyHealth case is the turning point.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Interpret how different executive roles translate the same strategy into divergent priorities that leave enterprise gaps unowned.
2. Evaluate the strategic and performance costs of unexamined bias in your organisation.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Say why this section matters.
Say: "Behavioural biases are systematic, predictable and cumulative. Left unmanaged, they act as a silent rot, compromising the integrity of even the most technically rigorous strategic frameworks."

2. Bridge to the opening question.
Say: "Let us zoom in on the functional landscape, where functional bias shows up."

slides.title: Zooming in functional landscape - Where functional bias shows up
slides.notes:
ZOOMING IN ON THE FUNCTIONAL LANDSCAPE · WHERE FUNCTIONAL BIAS SHOWS UP

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Ask the question on the slide.
Ask: "If every executive in your organisation performed perfectly within their own function, would your strategy actually deliver the result you intend?"
Hold the silence. Let the room sit with it before anyone answers.

2. Ask where functional bias shows up.
Ask: "Where do you see functional bias show up in your organisation?"
Listen for: delayed decisions, misaligned KPIs, teams working hard in different directions.

3. Name why it happens.
Say: "Functional bias does not appear on any dashboard, yet it shows up everywhere. Each executive function experiences the organisation through the variable it controls most directly."

4. Bridge to 3.1.
Say: "Let us watch it happen in a live case."

slides.title: 3.1 · Functional Bias In Action – MyHealth Live Case Study
slides.notes:
3.1 · FUNCTIONAL BIAS IN PRACTICE: THE MYHEALTH CASE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Explain the professional filter.
Say: "When a strategic direction is announced, every executive in the room hears the same words through their own professional filter. Years of professional training and experience shape how leaders interpret opportunity, risk and priority."
Say: "The CFO listens for financial exposure. The COO hears operational feasibility. The CHRO listens for capability implications. The CMO hears the customer promise. Each interpretation is rational. Each perspective is valuable. When these perspectives remain unspoken, functional bias begins quietly reshaping how the strategy is understood and acted upon."

2. Read the announcement aloud.
Read aloud: "To become the leading patient-centric provider, we are launching the 'MyHealth Live' Portal. It provides 24/7 digital access to data, cuts admin calls by 30%, and builds trust through transparency. We go live in 60 days."
Say: "The portal has three strategic objectives: 24/7 digital access for patients to their data; a 30% reduction in administrative calls; and greater patient trust through transparency."
Ask: "Before we explore the executive perspectives, what is your immediate reaction to this announcement?"

3. Take the room through the executive roles.
Ask each participant to choose the executive role on the slide closest to their own function or most relevant to their organisation, and to say what that executive hears and how they would define success. Ask them to hold that thought; you return to it when examining the tensions.
Use these as your reference points:
CEO (Managing Director): "We need a win. Speed is everything to keep our momentum." Success: launching ahead of the competition.
CFO (Finance Director): "How does this affect the bottom line? We need to offset the cost." Success: delivering 8% under budget with clear ROI.
COO (Operations Director): "Will this actually make the ER run smoother or just add more steps?" Success: reducing patient processing time by 22%.
CHRO (HR Director): "My people are tired. Can they handle another digital tool?" Success: 95% of staff feeling confident and trained.
CTO (IT Director): "One data leak and we're done. This has to be a fortress." Success: 100% uptime with zero security breaches.
CMO (Marketing Director): "If patients don't use it, it doesn't exist. We need adoption." Success: 90% of active patients registered within 90 days.
CCO (Commercial Director): "This is a growth engine. How do we turn clicks into consults?" Success: a 35% increase in digital bookings.
CPO (Procurement Director): "I need those vendor contracts signed yesterday to hit that 60-day mark." Success: seamless infrastructure and logistics delivered on time.
CRO (Risk Director): "Transparency is important, but privacy laws are non-negotiable." Success: zero compliance incidents or regulatory flags.
CSO (Strategy Director): "This portal is our first-mover advantage." Success: solidifying our position as the regional digital leader.
Ask: "Does this match what you would have been thinking?"

4. Move to the tensions.
Take two or three role combinations, for example CTO and CMO, or CEO and CHRO. Ask the participants who chose those roles to share again.
Ask: "Where do these two perspectives create friction?"
Then ask: "What happens if both leaders pursue their own definition of success without talking to each other?"
Example, say: "The CTO may prioritise maximum security while the CMO prioritises simplicity and ease of use. Both are pursuing legitimate outcomes, and the requirements of one may affect the ability of the other to succeed."

5. Say why this matters.
Say: "Every executive could deliver a result. The CFO could deliver the budget. The CTO could deliver security. The CMO could deliver adoption. The CHRO could deliver workforce readiness. The COO could deliver operational efficiency. And the organisation could still fail to achieve the intended enterprise outcome. If leaders do not surface how their contributions depend on, constrain or compete with one another, the strategy begins to fracture between functions."
Deepen, say: "Sustainable execution rarely depends on one dominant function. Value is produced when differentiated capabilities are deliberately integrated around a common purpose."
(Insight: Complementary capability. Source: Journal, 9 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

6. Introduce the White Space.
Say: "This brings us to the space between those functional contributions: the White Space. White Space is the gap between what individual functions successfully deliver and what the organisation needs those contributions to produce together."
Say: "Return to the MyHealth case. The portal launches. Technology delivers a secure and stable platform. Marketing achieves strong patient adoption. Operations delivers the required processes. HR trains the workforce. Finance keeps the programme within budget. The dashboards are green."
Say: "Then something unexpected happens. Emergency rooms experience a 40% spike in 'panic visits' from patients who receive raw, uninterpreted laboratory results at 9:00 pm on a Friday. Patient satisfaction falls because patients feel confused, anxious and unsupported. Everyone delivered. The enterprise outcome did not."
Say: "The problem did not sit neatly inside Technology, Marketing, Operations or any other single function. It sat between them. Who considered what happens emotionally when a patient receives a concerning result after hours? Who connects digital access to clinical interpretation? Who owns the hand-off between receiving information and knowing what to do with it?"
Say: "The White Space sits between functional mandates, where no one function is fully in charge, and where the customer experience, the dependencies and the enterprise outcome come together. It is where individually successful contributions must connect to produce the intended result."
Deepen, say: "Examine the interfaces where culture is actually tested: hand-offs between functions, resource conflicts, decision disagreements and responses to mistakes. These moments reveal whether people experience themselves as contributors to one whole or as representatives protecting separate territories."
(Insight: Where culture is tested. Source: Journal, 2 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

7. Read the three-point check aloud.
Read aloud: "One, Functional Success: does my 'done' create more work, or unintended consequences, for someone else? Two, White Space: if my dashboard is green but the customer, employee or another part of the system is red, where is the disconnect? Three, Enterprise Consequence: when all the contributions come together, has the enterprise actually won?"

8. Hold the key facilitation moment.
Ask: "In your current strategy, where is the enterprise consequence that nobody formally owns?"
This is often where the most candid and valuable conversation in the session occurs. Give it space.

9. Land it.
Say: "A green dashboard does not necessarily mean a successful strategy. The strategic question is whether our individual successes combine to produce the outcome we intended."
Deepen, say: "People can work in the same organisation, attend the same meetings and share the same corporate values while remaining separated by invisible walls: functional silos, hierarchy, professional status, historical conflict or assumptions about whose contribution matters most."
(Insight: Invisible walls. Source: Journal, 4 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Ask: "What invisible walls are preventing capable people from becoming an integrated organisation?"

10. Bridge to 3.2.
Say: "So why is all this important? Because the behaviours behind it carry a hidden cost, and in an organisation that cost becomes strategic."

slides.title: 3.2 · The Hidden Cost Of Poor Behavioural Awareness
slides.notes:
3.2 · THE HIDDEN COST OF POOR BEHAVIOURAL AWARENESS (5 STRATEGIC COSTS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Let the number land.
Ask: "If I told you that disciplined decision-making delivers approximately 6% higher returns than the norm, what would that mean in real terms for your organisation?"
Let the number land before proceeding.
Say: "Research by McKinsey & Company indicates that organisations with disciplined decision-making practices, specifically those that actively mitigate cognitive bias, deliver returns approximately 6% higher than their peers. Conversely, a lack of behavioural awareness creates a hidden tax on the organisation."
Say: "The question we are now asking is: what can biased thinking and behaviour actually cost the strategy?"

2. Cost 1: Misallocated Capital (Stability and Action Biases).
Say: "Resources go to the wrong places. Capital, people and management attention keep flowing towards investments that no longer offer the best future value, or towards new opportunities whose potential has been overestimated."
Ask: "Which biases could contribute, and how?"
Say: "Sunk-Cost bias keeps resources tied to an investment because so much has already been spent on it. The Endowment Effect causes leaders to overvalue businesses, assets or projects simply because the organisation already owns them. At the other extreme, Overconfidence and the Illusion of Control encourage ambitious investments or 'ego acquisitions' because leaders overestimate their judgement or their ability to control the outcome."
Say: "We can therefore misallocate capital in two directions: holding onto yesterday for too long, or betting too confidently on tomorrow. The strategic cost: resources are committed according to behavioural attachment or confidence, and future value is overlooked."
Deepen, say: "Cultures are revealed by their budget allocations and recognition rituals. List the three things the team has invested most resource in over the last quarter and the three things it has most publicly celebrated. If those lists do not match the stated values, the values on the wall are decoration."
(Insight: Where the resources go. Source: Journal, 26 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

3. Cost 2: Strategic Inertia (Stability Biases).
Say: "The organisation can see that change is needed, but struggles to move. The market may be changing, customer expectations shifting, new technology emerging. Leadership may even recognise these changes. Yet the organisation continues operating largely as before."
Ask: "Which biases could contribute, and how?"
Say: "Anchoring keeps thinking tied to old assumptions, measures or definitions of success. Status Quo bias makes the existing model feel safer simply because it is familiar. Loss Aversion makes leaders focus more strongly on what could be lost through change than on what could be gained. The fear of change stops the dominant coalition from shifting to new models, so the organisation keeps finding reasons to delay, protect or incrementally adjust what already exists."
Say: "The strategic cost: the organisation responds to a changing environment more slowly than the environment itself is changing."
Deepen, say: "Senior leaders accumulate programmes built to reproduce past breakthroughs. Identify one programme, ritual or initiative that exists mainly because something like it succeeded before, and pull the data on whether it still produces the original effect. If the case for keeping it is mostly nostalgia, schedule its sunset this quarter."
(Insight: Programmes that outlive their purpose. Source: Journal, 6 May 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)

4. Cost 3: Execution Failure (Action-Oriented Biases).
Say: "The strategy looks achievable on paper but breaks down during delivery. The organisation commits to outcomes, timelines and initiatives without sufficiently accounting for the conditions required to deliver them."
Ask: "Which biases could contribute, and how?"
Say: "Optimism bias encourages leaders to expect more favourable outcomes than the evidence supports. The Planning Fallacy causes teams to underestimate how much time, money, capability and coordination delivery will actually require. Overconfidence strengthens the belief that the organisation will somehow overcome those constraints. Once execution begins, action-reinforcing Confirmation bias makes leaders pay greater attention to evidence that the plan is working while explaining away early warning signs."
Say: "The strategic cost: the organisation commits beyond its realistic capacity to deliver, and recognises the gap too late. Some of that underestimated complexity sits between functions, in the White Space, as well as in the project plan."
Deepen, say: "Strategic outcomes are usually cumulative. Capability, trust, customer loyalty and operational discipline are built through repeated investments whose effects may not be immediately visible. Good execution distinguishes between an initiative that is failing and one whose results have not yet matured, while using evidence to test whether the underlying assumptions remain valid."
(Insight: Failing, or still maturing. Source: Journal, 1 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

5. Cost 4: Innovation Suppression (Social and Interest Biases).
Say: "Good ideas, alternative perspectives and uncomfortable truths struggle to survive inside the organisation. People may have ideas and still learn which ideas are safe to voice, which assumptions are dangerous to challenge, and whose thinking carries the greatest weight."
Ask: "Which biases could contribute, and how?"
Say: "Groupthink makes maintaining agreement more important than examining alternatives. Conformity bias encourages people to align with the dominant view. Authority bias makes people reluctant to challenge powerful or respected leaders. Career-Risk bias raises the personal cost of dissent: what happens to me if I challenge this and I am wrong? Valuable ideas may disappear before they are ever seriously considered."
Say: "The strategic cost: the organisation loses access to ideas and information that could have improved the strategy, because people learn to filter themselves."
Deepen, say: "Organisations often face the most intense resistance to necessary truth from the people who should be most invested in hearing it. Build the protection of truth-tellers into the structure of the culture as well as the values statement."
(Insight: Protect the truth-teller. Source: Journal, 7 February 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Ask: "How many ideas never reach the strategy table because people already know what the table wants to hear?"

6. Cost 5: Purpose Drift (Interest and Social Biases).
Say: "The organisation gradually starts making decisions that serve immediate interests while moving away from its longer-term strategic intent. Purpose drift is often gradual. Individual decisions can appear reasonable on their own, but over time they pull the organisation away from what it set out to achieve."
Ask: "Which biases could contribute, and how?"
Say: "Self-Interest bias can steer decisions towards protecting individual or functional interests. Incentive bias makes people optimise for what is measured and rewarded, even when that behaviour works against the wider strategy. The Halo Effect lets a highly visible success, influential leader or celebrated 'quick win' receive more strategic weight than the evidence warrants. Social pressure then reinforces the direction, because challenging something perceived as successful becomes increasingly difficult."
Say: "The strategic cost: short-term success begins to redefine what matters, and the organisation gradually loses alignment with its longer-term intent."
Deepen, say: "Drift happens through a series of small accommodations that go unchallenged. What is tolerated becomes what is normal, and by the time the values have shifted no one can point to the moment it happened. Leaders who want to protect what the organisation stands for must challenge early drift."
(Insight: Small accommodations. Source: Journal, 16 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

7. Ask which cost is most active.
Ask: "Which of these is the most expensive one in your organisation right now, and which is the most invisible?"
If time allows: put participants in pairs. Each pair identifies the cost it believes is most active and traces it back to a bias family from 2.4. Bring the pairs back for a short share-out.

8. Land the five costs.
Say: "Cognitive bias does not remain inside someone's head. It eventually shows up in the economics and performance of the organisation. Bias begins in judgement. Its cost appears in strategy."
Say: "Unexamined bias turns one strategy into competing functional priorities, and its cost shows in decisions, delays and lost value."

9. Bridge to Section 4.
Say: "Now that we know what bias costs, the next question is: where exactly in the strategy process do these costs accumulate? That is what Section 4 maps for us."

slides.title: Section 3 Reflections
slides.notes:
SECTION 3 REFLECTIONS

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the two reflections.
Say: "Section 3 closes with two reflections on your portal page."
Read aloud: "3.1: Select the executive leader role that is most relevant to you. What does the internal translation reveal about your own blind spots? Where is the 'White Space' in your organisation's current strategy — the gap between functional success and enterprise outcome?"
Read aloud: "3.2: Which of the five hidden costs is most visible in your current organisation? Can you trace it back to a specific bias family? What would it take to address it?"

2. Set the expectation for depth.
Say: "Name the White Space and the cost you actually see in your organisation, and trace each back to the bias behind it. Your reflections build the Learning Portfolio you receive at the end of the programme."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write each reflection on their portal page and select Save Reflection.

slides.title: Section 4 · Extrapolating — Where
slides.notes:
SECTION 4 · EXTRAPOLATING — WHERE
Where Behavioural Strategy Operates · 4.1 · 4.2

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
This is the most diagnostic section. Participants move from understanding bias conceptually to mapping where it shows up: across their own strategy process (4.1, the four phases) and in the emotional environment that either amplifies or dampens it (4.2.1 emotional climate, 4.2.2 emotional state, 4.2.3 the six debiasing principles). Expect this section to surface uncomfortable recognitions. That is the design intent.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Identify where bias and emotional climate most affect decision quality across the strategy process.
2. Determine the interventions that would most strengthen objectivity in your own strategy process.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Frame the section.
Say: "Every bias we explored in Section 2 has a home. It lives in specific moments of the strategy process. This section maps those moments."

2. Bridge to 4.1.
Say: "We start with the strategy journey itself."

slides.title: 4.1 · The Strategy Journey As A Bias Landscape
slides.notes:
4.1 · THE STRATEGY JOURNEY AS A BIAS LANDSCAPE (4 PHASES)

HOW TO TEACH IT:
Walk through the four phases as a group, in order. For each phase, teach the content, pause on its scanner question, then ask the phase question. If possible, capture the room's answers on a whiteboard or shared screen: this builds a live bias exposure map of the group's actual strategy processes.

1. Set up the landscape.
Say: "Strategy is designed by people and delivered by people. Throughout the strategy journey, people are required to interpret information, make sense of circumstances, generate possibilities, make choices, translate direction into their own contribution, coordinate with others and act. At every one of these moments, what people think, decide and do can influence the strategy."
Say: "Every strategic message is filtered through the mind and the heart. Bias therefore lives in processes as well as in people. More precisely, it enters at the specific moments within the strategy process where human judgement is required: where data must be interpreted, options imagined, choices made, and strategic intent translated into action."
Say: "This is the core insight of the Bias Landscape: behavioural strategy helps us identify where, across the strategy journey, human judgement is most exposed to invisible distortion, from the people shaping the strategy to the people delivering it. The four phases give us a practical way to examine that exposure."

2. Phase 1 · Diagnosis: wrong reality enters the strategy.
Say: "Every strategy begins with a reading of reality. Leaders scan the external environment, assess internal capability and form a view of what is true about the organisation's position. This diagnostic work is the foundation on which everything else is built. It is also where the first, and potentially most consequential, distortions can enter. The human mind cannot process all available information equally. It selects. And the criteria for selection are rarely completely objective."
Say: "Availability bias governs what gets noticed. Information that is recent, vivid or frequently discussed can receive far greater weight than its actual strategic significance; a competitor's recent product launch or a difficult quarter just closed can dominate the diagnostic conversation. Anchoring governs what gets used as a reference point: the first number on a slide, the previous year's result or an analyst's initial estimate becomes a gravitational centre around which later thinking orbits. Confirmation bias closes the loop: once leaders have formed an initial view, even provisionally, they seek and give greater weight to information that supports it."
Say: "A strategy built on a flawed diagnosis can become a well-organised response to a reality the organisation has misread."
Deepen, say: "Organisations misdiagnose problems when they address visible symptoms without examining the beliefs producing them. Persistent silo behaviour or poor accountability may survive new processes because the underlying assumptions remain intact. Ask what is happening, and what logic keeps making this behaviour reasonable to the people practising it."
(Insight: Diagnosis beneath visible behaviour. Source: Journal, 2 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Deepen, say: "Organisations often decide first and then use analysis to validate the decision. Sound strategy needs enough humility to let evidence alter the chosen path."
(Insight: Deciding first. Source: Journal, 17 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Read the scanner question: "If we stripped out everything our team already knew or believed before this process began, what would the remaining evidence actually tell us?"
Ask: "Is your current strategic diagnosis based on data you deliberately sought, or data that happened to be available?"

3. Phase 2 · Option Generation: the solution space is narrowed before debate.
Say: "Once the organisation has formed a view of reality, people begin asking: what could we do? What directions are available? This should be one of the most generative moments in strategy, where imagination, expertise and creative tension produce a range of possible paths. Yet the range of possibilities can begin narrowing before options are ever formally tabled. Social dynamics, professional filters and unspoken assumptions about what is realistic, acceptable or safe to propose all influence what reaches the table."
Say: "Status Quo bias is the most pervasive: the current strategy pulls thinking towards what already exists, so teams make small adjustments and leave bold options unexplored. Functional and Silo bias means options are generated inside each organisational lane, so the transformative options that need cross-functional integration are structurally disadvantaged. Career-Risk bias is perhaps the most damaging and least visible: radical options carry personal risk for the people who advocate them, so they do not get advocated; they may not even get thought. Groupthink and Conformity operate in the room itself: once a dominant view begins to form, the social pressure to align with it grows. Dissenting options require social courage as well as intellectual effort, and in most rooms courage is in shorter supply than intelligence."
Say: "The options that eventually reach a decision have already passed through human, professional and social filters."
Read the scanner question: "What is the most disruptive option we have not yet put on the table, and what is the real reason it is not there?"
Ask: "How many genuinely different strategic options did your team consider before committing to your current direction?"

4. Phase 3 · Decision: the chosen path becomes flawed or skewed.
Say: "Eventually, possibilities must become choices. Strategic decisions are rarely made in neutral conditions: there may be pressure to commit, uncertainty about outcomes, competing interests and differences in authority around the table. As the choice gets closer, the desire for certainty grows. Confidence can increase even when the evidence has not changed. Who holds authority, who is most respected and who has the most to gain or lose begin influencing the outcome alongside the evidence."
Say: "Overconfidence inflates the perceived quality of the preferred option; its advantages gain weight while its risks are progressively managed down. Loss Aversion tilts choices towards protecting what already exists. Authority bias and the Halo Effect influence whose judgement receives the greatest weight. The Sunk-Cost Fallacy and the Endowment Effect influence which portfolio options survive, because choices that write down previous investments or relinquish something the organisation has built are harder to make."
Deepen, say: "Organisations often continue weak initiatives because money, reputation or effort has already been invested, defending yesterday's choice at the expense of tomorrow's outcome. Sound strategy needs the courage to discontinue an unsuitable course, absorb the immediate cost and return to the principles that should govern the decision."
(Insight: The sunk-cost trap. Source: Journal, 22 July 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Say: "The moment of decision is often where the pressure to commit is highest and the tolerance for challenge is lowest."
Deepen, say: "Consequential decisions require leaders to separate facts from framing, individual interests from institutional interests, and genuine risk from manufactured urgency."
(Insight: Disciplined diagnosis. Source: Journal, 14 August 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Read the scanner question: "If the person who proposed this option had no stake in the outcome and no prior relationship with the team, would we make the same decision?"
Ask: "Who had the most influence over your last major strategic call, and was that influence based on evidence or authority?"

5. Phase 4 · Execution: strategy decays in delivery.
Say: "The strategy may have been shaped and decided by a relatively small group of people. It now has to be delivered through many more. People across the organisation must interpret what the strategy means for them, translate it into their own contributions, make day-to-day decisions, coordinate across functions, respond to changing conditions and act. The strategy continues to pass through human judgement long after the formal decision. Bias travels from planning into delivery."
Say: "The Planning Fallacy means the execution plan may already underestimate the time, resources and complexity required; interdependencies between teams stay underweighted until they surface in delivery. Confirmation bias, in its action-reinforcing form, shapes how execution signals are read: green indicators are noticed, amber ones rationalised, red ones attributed to temporary conditions, and by the time the evidence is undeniable the opportunity for correction has narrowed. Incentive bias fractures alignment: people deliver against their own measures while the enterprise outcome falls behind. Self-Interest and Functional bias fragment what the strategy requires to be integrated."
Deepen, say: "Senior teams routinely read good outcomes as evidence of sound process. A deal closes or a launch lands, and the messy path that produced it is quietly adopted as the method."
(Insight: Outcomes taken as proof. Source: Journal, 24 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Ask: "Pick one recent win. How did it actually happen, separately from what it produced?"
Say: "This is where the White Space from 3.1 becomes particularly important. People can perform successfully within their own mandates while the dependencies, hand-offs and competing requirements between those mandates remain unresolved. Through the decisions, interpretations and behaviours of execution, the people delivering the strategy continue shaping what it ultimately becomes."
Deepen, say: "Leaders have a responsibility to allocate work and to create line of sight between contribution and collective purpose. When people understand where they fit, responsibility becomes more meaningful and coordination becomes easier."
(Insight: Line of sight. Source: Journal, 3 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Say: "Execution failure can be a continuation of behavioural problems that entered earlier in the strategy journey, or the result of new behavioural dynamics emerging as more people engage with the strategy."
Read the scanner question: "As strategy moves through the organisation, how are people interpreting what it means for them, and are those interpretations and contributions coming together to produce the intended enterprise outcome?"
Ask: "How confident are you that people across your organisation understand what the strategy requires of them, and how their contribution connects with others?"

6. Land the four phases.
Say: "When we say that strategy is designed by people and delivered by people, behavioural strategy asks us to examine the human influences across that entire journey."
Ask: "At which of the four phases is your organisation currently most exposed?"
Participants often locate their organisation primarily in Phase 3 or 4. Take them back to Phase 1. Ask: "Was the diagnosis clean before the decision was ever made?"

7. Bridge to 4.2.
Say: "We have mapped where judgement is exposed. Now we turn to the heart: the emotional dimension of strategy."

slides.title: 4.2. The Emotional Dimension Of Strategy
slides.notes:
4.2 · THE EMOTIONAL DIMENSION OF STRATEGY · 4.2.1 · EMOTIONAL CLIMATE AS ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open with a one-word map of the room.
Ask: "In one word, what is the dominant emotional state in your leadership team's strategy conversations right now?"
Ask three or four participants. Write the words on a whiteboard or flip chart. This creates a live emotional map of the room before the framework is introduced.

2. Introduce the emotional dimension.
Say: "We have established that strategy is designed by people and delivered by people, and that every strategic message passes through two human filters: the mind and the heart. We now turn to the emotional dimension: how what people feel can influence how they think, engage and act around strategy."
Say: "People do not encounter strategy in an emotionally neutral state. They may experience it through confidence, fear, optimism, frustration, fatigue, anger or uncertainty. These emotional conditions influence how people interpret information, respond to challenge, perceive risk, engage with decisions and ultimately act. Emotion can shape strategy at both ends of the journey: in the leaders designing and deciding it, and in the people interpreting, translating and delivering it."
Say: "The emotional dimension asks us to examine three connected areas: the emotional climate surrounding strategy, the emotional states through which people experience strategy, and the practices that stop emotion and bias from distorting strategic judgement and action."

3. Teach the cabin-pressure picture.
Say: "The emotional climate of an organisation or team acts like atmospheric pressure around strategy. It shapes whether the organisation's Thinking Architecture can function effectively, or whether thinking becomes constrained, defensive or closed."
Say: "Think of cabin pressure in an aeroplane. When the pressure is right, you barely notice it; you simply function. When the pressure changes significantly, your ability to function can change with it. You may become uncomfortable or disoriented, and your judgement may eventually be affected. The person has not changed. The conditions around them have."
Say: "People also differ in their capacity to respond to changing pressure. A baby has less developed capacity to regulate and adapt to changes in cabin pressure. An adult is better able to recognise what is happening and take deliberate action to adjust."
Say: "Strategic pressure is inevitable. Leaders will face uncertainty, disagreement, challenge, competing interests and difficult choices. What matters is their capacity to remain effective within that pressure. This is why leaders must develop emotional maturity: the capacity to recognise and regulate their own emotional responses so that pressure does not unnecessarily distort how they think, decide or engage with others. And because leaders shape the conditions around them, how they respond under pressure contributes to the climate in which everyone else must think and operate."
Deepen, say: "When leaders become psychologically captured by a threat, organisations often inherit that preoccupation through excessive controls, defensive decisions or distorted priorities. Mature leadership keeps problems in proportion and preserves enough internal steadiness to continue exercising judgement."
(Insight: Alert without becoming absorbed. Source: Journal, 4 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Say: "As Quy Nguyen Huy's research suggests, emotions can act as gatekeepers to deliberate thinking. They influence whether people slow down to examine evidence, question assumptions and consider alternatives, or rely more heavily on instinctive and defensive responses."

4. Teach the three climates, one at a time.
Say: "We can think of three different atmospheric conditions around strategy. Each creates a different kind of emotional pressure on strategy and on people's thinking."
Say: "One: Fear-Dominated, the pressure to protect. The emotional driver is anxiety and defence: people focus on protecting themselves and worry about being blamed, punished or seen as wrong. The strategic outcome is Strategic Paralysis: the organisation becomes too careful, people choose safer options, avoid difficult decisions and are less willing to take necessary risks. The impact on thinking: threat narrows thinking. People keep quiet, agree with others or avoid challenging senior people, so important information and different ideas never enter the conversation. On the slide: System 1 hijack."
Deepen, say: "A technically correct leader can still generate fear, silence or defensive behaviour through the way they exercise authority. Leaders need to examine what their habitual responses create around them, alongside what their decisions accomplish."
(Insight: What authority creates. Source: Journal, 30 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Deepen, say: "The danger arises when internal anxiety begins governing external decisions. Fear can produce unnecessary control, rushed decisions, avoidance or constant changes in direction."
(Insight: Anxiety that governs decisions. Source: Journal, 3 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Ask: "Raise your hand if you have personally experienced this climate at any point in your career."
Say: "Two: Narcissism-Dominated, the pressure to validate. The emotional driver is ego and validation: people feel pressure to support the leader and their ideas, and agreement becomes easier than challenge. The strategic outcome is Strategic Delusion: the organisation becomes too confident in its own strategy, warning signs are ignored, weak assumptions go untested, and it may continue in the wrong direction because people are unwilling to question it. The impact on thinking: thinking becomes one-sided. People look for reasons the chosen direction is right and stop asking whether it could be wrong. On the slide: the validation loop."
Deepen, say: "When advisers reinforce the posture the leader already wants to adopt, the leadership team becomes an echo chamber. People learn that influence is gained through agreement, and the culture loses the ability to challenge damaging assumptions."
(Insight: The echo chamber. Source: Journal, 17 July 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Deepen, say: "Leaders who derive too much identity from position, recognition or being right can experience disagreement as a personal threat. Secure leaders have greater capacity to listen, share authority, acknowledge mistakes and recognise others. Inner security becomes an organisational capability."
(Insight: Secure identity. Source: Journal, 2 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Ask: "Raise your hand if you have personally experienced this climate."
Say: "Three: Grounded Confidence, the pressure to examine. The emotional driver is curiosity and security: people feel safe enough to ask questions, disagree and admit when they do not know something. The strategic outcome is Strategic Agility: the organisation can respond when things change, question its assumptions, learn from what is happening and adjust the strategy without losing direction. The impact on thinking: thinking stays open. People examine the evidence, consider different views and challenge assumptions, which makes it easier to spot weak thinking and bias before they affect important decisions. On the slide: System 2 optimisation."
Deepen, say: "In a crisis, organisations with a culture of calm, evidence-based thinking hold their nerve better than those that follow the emotional temperature of the room. Build the capacity for calm assessment before you need it."
(Insight: Calm before the crisis. Source: Journal, 13 January 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Ask: "Raise your hand if you have experienced this climate." Asking for hands on each climate normalises the conversation and reduces defensiveness.

5. Make the key facilitation point.
Read the banner aloud: "For a leader, managing the emotional climate is a fiduciary responsibility."
Say: "If you allow a climate of fear or narcissism to take root, you are effectively dismantling the organisation's ability to process reality."
Ask: "What does it cost your organisation when the climate is wrong, and who is accountable for that?"

6. Bridge to 4.2.2.
Say: "We now move from the emotional climate around people to the emotional state within people."

slides.title: 4.2.2a · Emotional Alignment: The State Of Being
slides.notes:
4.2.2a · EMOTIONAL ALIGNMENT: THE STATE OF BEING

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Move from climate to state of being.
Say: "This part moves from the macro climate to the individual and team emotional states that strategy lands into. It is practical and diagnostic, so apply it to a current project or decision as we go."
Say: "To make emotional climate actionable, it must move from an abstract organisational condition to something leaders can see, name and work with directly at the individual level. This shift happens through emotional alignment: the practice of identifying the specific state of being through which strategy is being experienced."

2. Teach Ekman's six basic emotions.
Point to the six faces on the left of the slide.
Say: "Strategy always lands into an emotional climate before it lands into action. Emotional alignment is achieved by explicitly naming the current emotional state through which strategy is being experienced. Leaders and teams operate from a dominant state of being, commonly expressed across Ekman's six basic emotions: joy, sadness, anger, fear, disgust and surprise."

3. Read the five factors, with a private rating after each.
Say: "Each state influences five factors. After each one, give your current team a private rating from 1 to 5. This becomes a personal baseline you can return to at the end of the unit."
Say: "Engagement Energy: the level of discretionary effort, momentum and willingness to contribute beyond minimum requirements."
Say: "Morale Drain: the degree to which emotional fatigue, disappointment or disengagement reduces capacity and persistence."
Deepen, say: "Cultures become healthier when people can voice concern, disappointment or uncertainty without being labelled negative or disloyal. Suppressed emotion moves underground."
(Insight: Suppressed emotion moves underground. Source: Journal, 5 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Say: "Friction Load: the amount of hidden resistance, tension or drag experienced in decisions, collaboration and follow-through."
Say: "Psychological Safety: the extent to which individuals feel safe to speak, challenge, admit uncertainty and take appropriate risk."
Deepen, say: "Part of an organisation's culture is what people believe will happen to them if they try something and it fails. Where the prevailing belief is that failure is punished, people stop trying, whatever the stated values say. Examine what people saw happen to the last person who took a risk and got it wrong."
(Insight: What happened to the last risk-taker. Source: Journal, 13 May 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Say: "Values Alignment: the consistency between stated values, observed leadership behaviour and everyday decisions under pressure."
Deepen, say: "An organisation may repeatedly communicate integrity, collaboration or accountability while rewarding behaviour that contradicts those values. Employees learn that the real culture is encoded in consequences. Culture becomes credible when what leaders praise publicly, tolerate privately and reward materially tells the same story."
(Insight: Culture encoded in consequences. Source: Journal, 1 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

4. Reinforce the key insight.
Say: "Unacknowledged emotional states silently override rational plans."
Ask: "What is the unacknowledged emotional state in your organisation's current strategy cycle?"
This is often the most candid question in the entire unit. Give it time.

5. Bridge to 4.2.2b.
Say: "The key is to make the emotional state observable. Leaders look for signals and then test what those signals mean. There are seven."

slides.title: 4.2.2b · Emotional Alignment: The State Of Being
slides.notes:
4.2.2b · EMOTIONAL ALIGNMENT: FROM EMOTION TO EVIDENCE · SIGNALS 1 TO 4

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the seven signals.
Say: "Make the emotional state observable: look for signals, then test what those signals mean. Here are the first four."

2. Signal 1 · Name the emotional state.
Say: "Name it, and invite correction."
Example, say: "There seems to be a lot of frustration around this strategy change. Is that a fair reading?"
Deepen, say: "Leaders do not strengthen people by pretending that fear, disappointment or grief do not exist. Mature leadership makes space for reality while helping people move from raw emotion towards reflection, meaning and renewed trust."
(Insight: Emotionally honest leadership. Source: Journal, 5 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)

3. Signal 2 · Ask directly.
Example, say: "What emotion best describes how you are experiencing this strategy right now: confidence, fear, frustration, excitement, uncertainty?"

4. Signal 3 · Observe behaviour.
Say: "A team that was previously vocal has become unusually quiet. The leader treats the silence as a signal and asks what is behind it."

5. Signal 4 · Notice where attention is going.
Say: "If people repeatedly focus on what could go wrong, fear may be directing attention towards risk and self-protection."

6. Bridge to the next three signals.
Say: "Three more signals sit in energy, language and behaviour."

slides.title: 4.2.2c · Emotional Alignment: The State Of Being
slides.notes:
4.2.2c · EMOTIONAL ALIGNMENT: FROM EMOTION TO EVIDENCE · SIGNALS 5 TO 7

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Signal 5 · Watch energy and challenge.
Say: "People attend meetings but contribute very little, deadlines start slipping and initiative falls. The leader explores whether disappointment or fatigue is draining morale. When discussions quickly become defensive or argumentative, anger or frustration may be increasing friction and reducing people's willingness to listen."

2. Signal 6 · Listen to the language.
Say: "Repeated comments such as 'What is the point?', 'They have already decided' or 'Just do what they want' can signal disappointment, frustration or disengagement."
Deepen, say: "Cultures that move straight from 'here is what changed' to 'here is what we need you to do next' produce resistance they cannot explain. The resistance signals that people do not yet feel understood. In a restructure, a strategic pivot or a change in leadership, listening is the load-bearing wall."
(Insight: Listen before you reframe. Source: Journal, 25 June 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

3. Signal 7 · Connect emotion to behaviour.
Example, say: "We have identified frustration as the dominant emotion. Where are we seeing that frustration show up: in collaboration, decision-making, effort or willingness to speak?"

4. Close on Name → Observe → Connect.
Say: "Name: what are people feeling? Observe: what are people doing? Connect: how might that emotional state be shaping what people notice, avoid, say or do?"
Say: "What are people feeling, and what is that feeling causing them to pay attention to, avoid or do?"
Deepen, say: "The leader who has no outlet for genuine emotion carries it into every decision. The leader who processes it appropriately can remain clear-headed in the most emotionally charged situations."
(Insight: Emotion processed in the right place. Source: Journal, 27 January 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)

5. Ask for a signal from the room.
Ask: "Which of these seven signals have you seen in your own team in the last month, and what did it tell you?"

6. Bridge to 4.2.3.
Say: "Awareness alone does not change outcomes. The goal now is to change how we design our strategy processes."

slides.title: 4.2.3 · Six Principles For Debiasing Strategy
slides.notes:
4.2.3 · SIX PRINCIPLES FOR DEBIASING STRATEGY

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the part.
Say: "The goal now is to change how we design our strategy processes. This is where the unit becomes actionable."
Say: "Awareness alone does not change outcomes. Without deliberate intervention, the same biases will continue to shape strategic conversations and decisions. What matters is how strategy processes are designed: who speaks, how options are generated, how challenge is introduced and how decisions are tested. These design choices determine whether thinking becomes clearer or more distorted."
Deepen, say: "A common and costly strategic failure is acting at the speed of assumption on information that was heard and never confirmed. Build an explicit verification step into decision-making before any significant response."
(Insight: Verification before response. Source: Journal, 13 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)
Say: "The six principles on the slide, adopted from the work of Kahneman, Lovallo, Sibony, Huy, Lencioni and Edmondson, give practical ways to strengthen the quality of the strategy management process. Each one closes with a simple rule."

2. Principle 1 · Separate ideation from evaluation.
Say: "When generating ideas, let the ideas come first and judge them later. Early criticism can stop people from sharing different or bold options. First create as many useful options as possible. Then evaluate them, compare them and decide which are strongest. Simple rule: generate first, evaluate afterwards."

3. Principle 2 · Name the emotional temperature before the strategic content.
Say: "Before an important strategy, performance or review conversation, check what people are feeling. Ask: what emotions are people bringing into this discussion that could affect how we think? Naming emotions such as fear, frustration, excitement or disappointment reduces hidden tension and helps people think and speak more openly. Simple rule: name the emotional climate in the room before discussing what is on the table."

4. Principle 3 · Assign a designated challenger role.
Say: "For important decisions, give someone the clear role of challenging the group's thinking: questioning assumptions, testing the preferred view and raising other explanations or options. Rotate the role so that challenge becomes a normal part of decision-making. It helps the team find blind spots before they become problems. Simple rule: give someone permission to challenge the thinking."
Deepen, say: "Most flawed plans survive because dissent was quietly designed out of the room. Before the next significant decision, invite the one person most likely to disagree and hear them out fully."
(Insight: Designated challenger. Source: Journal, 5 June 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)

5. Principle 4 · Use pre-mortem analysis as standard practice.
Say: "Before a major decision or an important initiative, imagine that it has already failed. Ask: if this fails, what are the most likely reasons? Then identify what could be done now to prevent those problems. Simple rule: imagine failure before it happens, and learn from it early."

6. Principle 5 · Make the reference class visible.
Say: "Judge a plan against what happened in similar situations as well as what the team believes will happen. Ask: what happened when other organisations or teams tried something similar under similar conditions? Use that evidence when setting targets, estimating time and resources, and reviewing performance. It reduces overconfidence and keeps decisions grounded in reality. Simple rule: look outside before predicting what will happen inside."

7. Principle 6 · Create after-action protocols.
Say: "Build regular learning reviews into execution, during the strategy or project as well as at the end. Ask: what happened? What did we expect? What have we learned? What should we change? Use what the team learns to adjust decisions and actions while there is still time to improve the result. Simple rule: learn while you can still change the outcome."
Deepen, say: "Recurring problems treated as isolated events return. Reviews create little value when lessons remain conversational. Insight must eventually alter decisions, controls, resource allocation and expected behaviour."
(Insight: Lessons that change something. Source: Journal, 10 August 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

8. Ask each participant to choose the most absent principle.
Ask the room to read the six principles on the slide silently and choose the one most absent from their current practice.
Ask: "Which principle does your organisation consistently skip, and what does that cost you?"
Then ask: "Which one could you introduce into your very next strategy meeting without needing anyone's permission?"

9. Close the Extrapolating section.
Say: "Every phase of the strategy journey carries its own biases, and the emotional climate decides whether leaders surface them or defend them."
Ask: "You have now mapped where your organisation is most exposed and why. What is the one thing you are most committed to changing?"
Allow a brief pair share.

10. Bridge to Section 5.
Say: "Section 5 examines how leadership teams turn individual thinking into collective intelligence."

slides.title: Section 4 Reflections
slides.notes:
SECTION 4 REFLECTIONS

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the reflections.
Say: "Section 4 closes with three reflections on your portal page."
Read aloud: "4.1: At which of the four phases is your organisation currently most exposed? Use the scanner question for that phase to frame your answer. What would it mean for your strategy process if you addressed that phase more deliberately?"
Read aloud: "4.2.1: Which climate type best describes your team or organisation right now? What specific leadership behaviours are creating or sustaining that climate? What is the cost of that climate to the quality of your strategy work?"
Read aloud: "4.2.3: Which of these six principles do you currently apply most consistently? Which is most absent from your current practice? What would it look like to introduce one of the absent principles into your next important decision or meeting?"

2. Set the expectation for depth.

slides.title: Section 5 · Integration — Collective
slides.notes:
SECTION 5 · INTEGRATION — COLLECTIVE
How to Build Collective Intelligence · 5.1 · 5.2

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
This section is where the unit moves from diagnosis to design. Participants have identified what behavioural strategy is, why it matters and where biases operate. Now they learn how to build an environment where collective intelligence can actually function: the opening context (Me becomes We), the three pillars of integration (5.1) and the institutional practices (5.2). This is the most practically actionable section; treat it that way.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Recognise the conditions that turn individual perspectives into collective intelligence within a leadership team.
2. Prioritise the organisational practices that would most strengthen collective decision quality.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Frame the transition.
Say: "Everything we have covered so far reveals the problem. This section is about the solution architecture. It designs better environments for judgement."

2. Bridge to the opening context.
Say: "We start with what integration means."

slides.title: Creating Collective Intelligence for Execution
slides.notes:
CREATING COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE FOR EXECUTION · OPENING CONTEXT

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open with the question.
Ask: "If everyone in your leadership team performed at their personal best, would the quality of your collective decisions improve as a result?"
The expected answer is yes. The correct answer is: not necessarily. Allow the tension to sit before you teach the content.

2. Teach the thinking environment.
Say: "The quality of strategy execution is a direct function of the quality of the thinking environment: the conditions under which thinking happens."
Say: "In the Integration section, we solve the Elephant Perspective problem. We move from functional silos to an enterprise-wide perspective. This requires shifting the leadership team from 'Defending the Part' to 'Designing the Whole'."

3. Land the key shift.
Read the line on the slide: "Integration is where the 'Me' becomes 'We'."
Say: "It is the process of trading individual opinions for collective intelligence."
Deepen, say: "A healthy culture creates conditions in which different contributions can genuinely be joined together. This requires a shared identity strong enough to transcend functional identity, relationships strong enough to carry disagreement, and an understanding that no single part can independently produce the whole organisational outcome."
(Insight: Joining different contributions. Source: Journal, 4 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Ask: "What does your current strategy process do to actively create that shift, or does it assume it will happen naturally?"

4. Pose the diagnostic question.
Read the question on the slide: "At which phase in your current strategy process are you most exposed?"
Say: "Where is the quality of your thinking least protected? The answer to that question is where your debiasing effort should begin."
Ask participants to answer it privately in writing before you move to 5.1.

5. Bridge to 5.1.
Say: "Three pillars give us a practical framework for building collective intelligence."

slides.title: 5.1 · The Three Pillars Of Integration
slides.notes:
5.1 · THE THREE PILLARS OF INTEGRATION

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Surface the barriers first.
Ask: "Without looking at the screen, what do you think the biggest structural barrier to genuine collective intelligence is in your organisation?"
Take three or four responses. As you teach each pillar, show how the framework responds to the barriers the room has named.

2. Introduce the pillars.
Say: "Three pillars provide a practical framework for building collective intelligence in your leadership environment. Let us explore how each one fosters it."

3. Pillar 1 · Cognitive Integration: connecting the dots.
Say: "This is about breaking down the 'I'm an expert in my area' silos. If Marketing only sees customers and Finance only sees costs, they are both looking at a fragmented reality."
Say: "The goal: build a single version of the truth. How it works: you require every department to explain how its information affects everyone else. In practice: a stress test where the team asks, 'If the Finance data is right, does the Marketing plan still make sense?'"
Deepen, say: "The most accurate intelligence about what the organisation's decisions are producing is often held by those furthest from the decision-making centre. Build explicit structures that bring this intelligence from the edges into the rooms where decisions are made."
(Insight: Intelligence from the edges. Source: Journal, 2 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)
Ask: "Is this pillar present in your current strategy process, and if so, what does it look like in practice?"

4. Pillar 2 · Behavioural Guardrails: putting up safety nets.
Say: "Smart people make bad choices when they rush. Guardrails are simple rules that force your brain to slow down and switch from gut feel, System 1, to logic, System 2."
Say: "The goal: stop the loudest voice or the fastest talker from winning by default. How it works: you build friction into the meeting; you make it a requirement to disagree before a final vote is taken. In practice: the Challenge Clock, where you dedicate ten minutes to finding only reasons why the plan won't work."
Deepen, say: "Leaders who decide by who is loudest in the room, ahead of what is most true in the data, consistently make poor calls. Good judgement goes beneath the surface presentation and the political pressure to what is actually true."
(Insight: The loudest voice. Source: Journal, 14 January 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Ask: "Is this pillar present in your current strategy process, and what does it look like?"

5. Pillar 3 · Emotional Stabilisation: clearing the air.
Say: "If a room is full of fear or big egos, no one tells the truth. Stabilisation is about making the environment safe enough for high-level thinking."
Say: "The goal: move the team from defensiveness to curiosity. How it works: leaders admit they don't have all the answers. This lowers the atmospheric pressure and lets the team speak up without fear of looking bad. In practice: naming the feeling. Start by saying, 'I know we may all be anxious about this deadline. Let's acknowledge that before we look at the numbers.'"
Deepen, say: "Leadership maturity includes the ability to acknowledge uncertainty without transferring anxiety throughout the organisation. Steadiness means remaining sufficiently grounded to assess reality clearly and respond proportionately."
(Insight: Steadiness. Source: Journal, 3 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Ask: "Is this pillar present in your current strategy process, and what does it look like?"

6. Identify the weakest pillar.
Ask each participant to identify privately which pillar is most underdeveloped in their current environment. Invite three or four to share their answer and their reason. This is often the most direct conversation in the section.

7. Land the interdependence.
Read the banner aloud: "The pillars reinforce each other."
Say: "A strong Cognitive Integration process will collapse in a fear-dominated climate: that is a Pillar 3 failure. Guardrails will be bypassed if there is no psychological safety to use them: Pillar 3 again."

8. Bridge to 5.2.
Say: "The principles in 4.2.3 told you what to do. The institutional practices tell you how to embed it structurally, so it does not depend on one person's intention or memory."

slides.title: 5.2.1 · Neutralising Bias in the Strategy Room
slides.notes:
5.2.1 · INSTITUTIONAL PRACTICES FOR COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE · IN THE STRATEGY ROOM

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the ten practices.
Say: "The institutional practices are what must exist in the organisation for good thinking to happen consistently. They are structural changes to how strategy is conducted. There are ten: five in the strategy room and five in leadership culture."
Say: "In the strategy room is about how you design meetings and decision processes to reduce bias while people are making strategic decisions. As I go through each one, mark for yourself whether it is already active, partially active or absent in your organisation."

2. 72-Hour Pre-Read Mandate (neutralises Anchoring).
Say: "Strategic documents are distributed three days before the session. This prevents anchoring to the presenter's live framing and allows for independent reflection."

3. Rotating Neutral Facilitation (neutralises Authority Bias and Groupthink).
Say: "Sessions are led by someone other than the CEO or the most senior executive. This neutralises authority bias and groupthink by decoupling power from the process."
Deepen, say: "Leaders who assume strategic insight belongs only to the senior tier miss what the rest of the organisation sees. The next strategic insight may come from the youngest person on the team."
(Insight: Insight from every level. Source: Journal, 29 March 2026 — Professional Insights)

4. Blind Ideation (neutralises Conformity and the Halo Effect).
Say: "Ideas and critiques are submitted anonymously during the exploration phase. This removes conformity bias and the halo effect of senior-led suggestions."
Deepen, say: "Cultures become vulnerable when prestige determines whose ideas matter. Healthy cultures combine competence with humility and value overlooked contributors."
(Insight: Halo Effect. Source: Journal, 31 August 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

5. The Challenge Clock (neutralises the Action-Oriented rush).
Say: "A dedicated, non-negotiable segment on the agenda for dissenting views. It forces System 2 engagement and protects against the action-oriented rush to decide."

6. Silent Deliberation (neutralises Availability Bias).
Say: "Individual written reflection is required before any verbal group discussion. This prevents the 'first voice' from dominating and triggering availability bias."

7. Bridge to 5.2.2.
Say: "The second five practices sit in leadership culture."

slides.title: 5.2.2 · In Leadership Culture
slides.notes:
5.2.2 · INSTITUTIONAL PRACTICES FOR COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE · IN LEADERSHIP CULTURE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame leadership culture.
Say: "In leadership culture is about building leadership habits and organisational practices that reduce bias over time. Keep marking each practice as active, partially active or absent."

2. Public Cognitive Humility (neutralises Overconfidence).
Say: "Leaders explicitly share past errors and the logic used to correct them. This reduces overconfidence and models a culture of continuous learning."
Deepen, say: "Teams that only ever hear the polished version stop believing any of it. Name one of your own missteps openly to the people you lead; the candour builds the credibility that spin erodes."
(Insight: The polished version. Source: Journal, 22 May 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)
Deepen, say: "When something goes wrong, positional power makes it easy to locate failure elsewhere: in the team, the environment, the systems or the execution. Ask 'Who failed?' and also 'What did my decisions, assumptions, signals or omissions make possible?'"
(Insight: Self-examination. Source: Journal, 1 October 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)

3. Behavioural 360s (neutralises Self-Interest and Perspective).
Say: "Leadership assessments that measure self-awareness and decision-making rigour. They address self-interest and perspective bias through external feedback loops."

4. Debiasing Coaching (neutralises System 1 dominance).
Say: "Professional development focused on identifying personal 'cognitive signatures'. It builds the muscle for System 2 thinking under high-pressure conditions."

5. Safety Metrics (neutralises Innovation Suppression and Career-Risk).
Say: "Psychological safety surveys used as a lead indicator for strategy quality. They guard against innovation suppression and career-risk bias."

6. Strategic Post-Mortems (neutralises Hindsight Bias).
Say: "Radical transparency about why a strategy succeeded or failed. It dismantles hindsight bias and builds a database of organisational learning."
Deepen, say: "Shame is what cultures produce when failure is punished and never processed. When people are more afraid of being found wrong than of being wrong, they hide problems until those problems become crises. Build a culture where people can say 'I got this wrong' before it becomes 'we failed'."
(Insight: Saying "I got this wrong". Source: Journal, 6 January 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

7. Debrief.
Ask: "Which practice is most immediately implementable in your organisation without needing a mandate from above? What is stopping you from introducing it in your next meeting?"

8. Prioritise.
Ask each participant to select their top two or three practices and share one with the group, together with the bias it directly addresses. This connects the institutional practices back to the bias families of 2.4.

9. Close the section.
Say: "Collective intelligence emerges when leadership teams build practices that bring diverse perspectives into every strategic decision."

10. Bridge to Section 6.
Say: "In Section 6 you assess your own bias profile, and each group sets out the challenge it will address in its Problem Charter."

slides.title: Section 5 Reflections
slides.notes:
SECTION 5 REFLECTIONS

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the three reflections.
Say: "Section 5 closes with three reflections on your portal page."
Read aloud: "Opening context: What does 'integration' currently look like in your organisation? Where does the transition from individual perspectives to a shared enterprise view most often break down?"
Read aloud: "5.1: Which of the three pillars is most underdeveloped in your current team or organisation? What is one specific practice from that pillar that you could introduce in your next strategy meeting or working session?"
Read aloud: "5.2: Which two or three institutional practices are most immediately implementable in your context? What resistance might you encounter, and how would you address it?"

2. Set the expectation for depth.
Say: "Name a real practice and a real meeting where you will use it. Your reflections build the Learning Portfolio you receive at the end of the programme."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write each reflection on their portal page and select Save Reflection.

slides.title: Section 6 · Application — In Practice
slides.notes:
SECTION 6 · APPLICATION — IN PRACTICE
Behavioural Strategy in Practice · 6.1 · The Problem Charter

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
This is the application section. Participants first turn the unit's learning on themselves in the Self Reflection Bias Assessment (6.1), individually and in silence. Each group then creates its simulated company, names the trigger for redesigning its strategy and writes its Problem Charter, which opens the Capstone.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Assess your own leadership conduct against the behavioural conditions for sound strategic judgement.
2. Commit to the development priority with the greatest effect on your strategic judgement.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Say what the section does.
Say: "Sections 1 to 5 showed how bias shapes the way leaders think, decide and behave, and how the thinking environment a leader creates protects or weakens judgement. Section 6 turns that learning on you, and then on your group."

2. Introduce 6.1, the Self Reflection Bias Assessment.
Say: "The Self Reflection Bias Assessment shows how consistently your own leadership practice holds the behavioural conditions for sound strategic judgement today. It covers five areas, with four statements in each: A1 · I Know My Biases; A2 · I Manage My Emotional Impact; A3 · I Build Psychological Safety; A4 · I Use Process to Protect Quality; A5 · I Treat People as the Strategy."
Say: "You score each statement from 1 to 5: 1 is rarely or never, 2 occasionally, 3 sometimes, 4 often, 5 consistently. The results give an overall score out of 100, a score for each area, and the area where you are most exposed: your development priority as you lead your simulated executive team through CESI."
Say: "The score bands are: 85–100 Leading Practice; 65–84 Established Awareness; 45–64 Developing Awareness; 25–44 Emerging Awareness; 20–24 At Risk."

3. Introduce the Problem Charter.
Say: "Each group then creates the simulated company it will lead as an executive team for the rest of CESI, names the change that means its current strategy no longer delivers, and writes its Problem Charter. The confirmed Charter becomes Section 1 of your group's Capstone S2R® Blueprint. From Unit 2 onwards, every section of the Blueprint is built for this company."

4. Bridge to the portal work.
Say: "Here is how the two parts run on your portal page."

slides.title: Section 6 · On the Portal
slides.notes:
SECTION 6 · ON THE PORTAL

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Set up the Self Reflection Bias Assessment.
Read aloud: "Score what is consistently true of your practice right now. The value of this tool is entirely dependent on your honesty."
Allow silence to settle before participants begin.
Say: "The assessment is done individually and in silence. Work through each of the five area tabs, A1 to A5, and score yourself 1 to 5 on each statement."
Allow completion without interruption.
Deepen, say: "Leaders need mechanisms that reveal their blind spots as well as their strengths. Acknowledging difficulty deepens trust when it comes with responsibility, learning and perseverance."
(Insight: A1 · I Know My Biases. Source: Journal, 14 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)

2. Read the results.
Say: "Open the Summary tab. Your overall score and its level appear there. Read the interpretation for your level before we discuss anything."
Caution: do not ask participants to share their overall score publicly. Say explicitly before the debrief: "The assessment is a personal diagnostic. Share only what you are comfortable sharing."

3. Debrief with three questions.
Ask: "What did your score reveal that surprised you?"
Then ask: "Which single area had the lowest sub-score, and what does that tell you?"
And finally: "What is one concrete action you will take before your next strategy session based on what this assessment surfaced?"
Say: "Self-assessment is the beginning of the work. The most useful thing you can do with this tool is to share what it surfaced with someone who observes you closely, and to let that become a real conversation."

4. Introduce the Problem Charter.
Post the challenge question in the chat and read it aloud: "How can an organisation strengthen its capability to design strategy, execute it through people and performance systems, and sustain results through the appropriate organisational environment?"

5. Explain the four steps.
Say: "Step 1, create your simulated company: its name, sector or industry, approximate size and main activity or service. Record your simulated executive team: each member and the executive role assigned to them, up to ten roles, each role held by one member."
Say: "Step 2, our strategy redesign trigger: agree the one change that means your company's current strategy no longer delivers. Record its source, internal or external, what has happened, and the signal that shows it cannot be ignored."
Say: "Step 3, our shared reality, in three tasks. Task 1: list at least two challenges the trigger has posed, or will pose, in each of strategy design, strategy execution and sustaining performance, drawing on what you have seen in your own work. Task 2: under each challenge, tick the others that solving it would also improve; the challenge that improves the most becomes your problem for that area. Task 3: for each problem, state why it matters now: how it stops the company from dealing with its trigger."
Say: "Step 4, our central organisational problem: one statement in four parts. What your trigger means you must now achieve; why you cannot, with your strategy design problem leading to your execution and sustaining performance problems; what this is costing, with a measure; and your challenge: how your company will build the capability to resolve the three problems, addressing your trigger. This statement directs your whole Capstone."

6. Explain the group record.
Say: "Your group chooses a scribe for this work. The scribe types what the group agrees, and the entries appear on every member's page. When the Charter is complete, each member reads it and selects Agree. When every member has agreed, the Charter feeds Section 1 of your team's Capstone S2R® Blueprint."

7. Send the groups to work.
Send the groups to their break-out rooms.

LATER, WHEN THE GROUPS DO THE WORK ON THE PORTAL:
Your role is to guide how the work is completed. The Charter is Capstone work and is assessed independently at the capstone. Help groups tie every challenge to their trigger, choose their scribe, complete all four steps in order and reach Agree from every member.

slides.title: Unit Summary · Return to the opening question
slides.notes:
UNIT SUMMARY · RETURN TO THE OPENING QUESTION

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the summary aloud.
Read the summary aloud, or ask a participant to read it. It is intentionally compact; it crystallises the arc of the unit. Do not add to it. Let it do its work.
Read aloud: "Unit 1, Behavioural Strategy Fundamentals, establishes the psychological bedrock that underpins all strategic decision-making. It opens by defining behavioural strategy as the intersection of cognitive psychology and strategic management, making the case that strategy is a deeply human exercise shaped by invisible mental filters. The unit introduces Kahneman's dual-process framework, System 1 fast thinking and System 2 deliberate thinking, as the core framework through which leaders should understand their own judgement."
Read aloud: "From there, it maps 20 cognitive biases across four families, Action-Oriented, Stability, Interest and Social, showing how each distorts strategic decisions in predictable, measurable ways, and what the organisational warning signs look like in practice."
Read aloud: "The unit then traces where these biases show up across the four phases of any strategy process: Diagnosis, Option Generation, Decision and Execution, demonstrating that bias is a process vulnerability. It adds a second dimension through the emotional climate, showing how fear, ego or grounded confidence in a leadership environment either amplifies or dampens the quality of thinking."
Read aloud: "It closes with practical intervention: six debiasing principles, three pillars for building collective intelligence, and institutional practices for embedding behavioural discipline, culminating in a self reflection bias assessment across five areas and each group's Problem Charter."
Read aloud: "The central argument of the unit, in one line: the quality of your strategy is a direct function of the quality of the thinking environment in which it was made."

2. Return to the opening question.
Ask two or three participants: "What has shifted in your understanding of how you think and make decisions as a leader?"

3. Close the room.
Ask each participant to complete the sentence on the slide privately in writing: "The one thing I am taking from this unit that I intend to act on is…"
Invite two or three to share voluntarily. This is the unit's final anchoring moment.

4. Bridge to Module 2.
Say: "Each of you now knows where your judgement needs support, and each group has the challenge it will lead through every later unit. Module 2, Direction, begins with Unit 2, Strategy Visioning and Success in Practice, where each group defines the strategy of the simulated company set out in its Problem Charter. The behavioural awareness you developed here is the filter through which all the strategy work that follows should pass."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants select "Unit 1 Complete" at the end of the unit page.
